projectTitle: Cascade Ridge Outfitters: The Report Nobody Could Actually Read
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish Salesforce admin build for a fictional outdoor gear company -- a real warranty claim object taken from data model through security, Flow automation, and reporting, then a genuine role-hierarchy mistake that quietly blocked two regional managers from seeing their own teams' records, found and fixed after go-live.
businessContext: Cascade Ridge Outfitters is an outdoor gear manufacturer/retailer running Salesforce for about 150 users across Sales and Service. Customers submit warranty claims on defective gear, but there's no real object or process for tracking them -- claims live in email threads and a shared spreadsheet, go missing, and age past any reasonable SLA until a customer escalates. Marisol Fontaine (VP of Customer Service) and Devon Okafor (the Salesforce Administrator) build Warranty_Claim__c end to end -- but a role-hierarchy mistake leaves Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren, the two regional Service Managers, unable to see their own teams' claims for weeks after go-live, even though the org-wide default and sharing rule are both configured correctly.
architectureSummary: A custom object, Warranty_Claim__c, with fields for status, product, claim amount, and region, related to Account and Contact. Org-Wide Default set to Private, with a role-hierarchy-based sharing rule intended to give each regional manager visibility into their own team's claims. A Record-Triggered Flow auto-routes new claims to the right regional service queue. Reports and a dashboard give Service leadership a by-region, by-status, aging-past-SLA view. The real defect wasn't in the sharing rule or the OWD -- it was in the Role Hierarchy itself, where the two regional managers were placed as peers of their own reps instead of above them, which silently starved the correctly-built sharing rule of anything to extend.

lessons.title: Meeting Cascade Ridge: Warranty Claims Nobody Can Track
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: Cascade Ridge's warranty claims live in email threads and a shared spreadsheet, go missing, and age past any reasonable SLA with nobody noticing until a customer escalates -- and what you have to learn about the business and the org before you can design anything to fix it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish Salesforce admin build for a fictional outdoor gear manufacturer and retailer, **Cascade Ridge Outfitters** -- roughly 150 Salesforce users split across Sales and Service. Cascade Ridge sells gear that sometimes fails under real use: a jacket zipper splits, a tent pole snaps, a sleeping bag's insulation gives out. When that happens, the customer is owed a warranty claim -- a real review of what went wrong and, where it's warranted, a resolution. Right now, none of that lives in Salesforce at all. A claim starts as an email to a service rep, gets copied by hand into a shared spreadsheet so 'someone' can keep track of it, and from there it's anyone's guess what happens next. Claims get lost between inboxes, nobody clearly owns a given claim once the original rep goes on vacation or moves teams, and there's no way to know a claim has been sitting untouched for three weeks until the customer calls back angry.

This video starts exactly where this kind of project always has to start: not with an object, not with a field, but with a meeting where you find out precisely what the business problem is, who feels it, and how the work actually happens today. You, **Devon Okafor**, are Cascade Ridge's Salesforce Administrator. **Marisol Fontaine**, VP of Customer Service, is the business sponsor who called this meeting -- she wants warranty claims actually tracked, clearly owned, and resolved on time, not quietly lost in somebody's inbox until a customer forces the issue. By the end of this series, Cascade Ridge has a real `Warranty_Claim__c` object, a security model that shows the right people the right claims and nobody else, automation that routes every claim to the correct region, and reporting Service leadership can actually trust. This lesson is step one: understanding the problem, in writing, before touching any setup menu.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your school has a lost-and-found, except there is no actual box. When someone loses a jacket, they tell a teacher, the teacher writes it on a sticky note, and the sticky note goes... somewhere. Maybe it's stuck to the bulletin board. Maybe it fell behind the bookshelf. Maybe three different teachers each wrote their own sticky note about the very same lost jacket, and nobody can tell which note is the real one, or if any of them are still true. Weeks later, a parent calls the school asking where the jacket is, and nobody can answer, because there was never one real, trustworthy place where 'lost jacket' actually lived.

That's Cascade Ridge's warranty claims today. A customer's broken tent pole or ripped jacket is like that lost jacket -- it gets written down in an email here, a spreadsheet row there, and nothing ties those together or makes sure one specific person is responsible for finding an answer. Marisol Fontaine's whole job is making sure customers get taken care of, but she can't do that for a problem that doesn't have one real home. Your job starts with sitting down with her and understanding exactly how messy it really is, before you try to build the box.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters most in this discovery meeting isn't the headline -- 'claims live in email and a spreadsheet' -- it's the specific failure modes that fall out of that arrangement: no single system of record, no enforced ownership, no visibility into age against any SLA, and no reliable way to even count how many claims are open right now. A spreadsheet can look like tracking without providing any of the three things a real tracking system needs: a durable record per claim, a clear owner, and a way to measure elapsed time. None of those exist today, which is why claims don't just get delayed -- they disappear entirely until a customer escalates and forces someone to go searching.

That's why this discovery meeting has to get specific about Cascade Ridge's actual Salesforce footprint, not just the pain. Cascade Ridge runs Salesforce for roughly 150 users split across Sales and Service. Service already has solid Account and Contact data for every customer -- that part of the model doesn't need to be touched. What's missing is any object at all for the claim itself: there's no `Warranty_Claim__c`, no related list on the Account showing a customer's claim history, nothing a report could ever be built against. Two Service regions already exist organizationally -- West, led by Hannah Reyes, and East, led by Tobias Lindgren -- but Salesforce has no concept of that structure applied to warranty work today, simply because there's no warranty object for a region to apply to yet. Getting all of this precisely right now, in writing, is what keeps the requirement in the next lesson honest about what's actually broken versus what merely feels messy.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down what you'd need to confirm, not just what you expect to hear:

- Is a shared spreadsheet really the only tracking mechanism, or are there side-channels (a service rep's personal notes, a manager's own tally) that never get captured anywhere official?
- Does any existing Salesforce object already come close to fitting a warranty claim, or does this genuinely need something new?
- Who actually owns a claim today, and what happens to it when that person is out?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the real problem in Marisol's own words

```
MARISOL: By the time a customer calls back asking where their claim
         went, we've usually already failed them once. We have no
         real way to see how many warranty claims are open right
         now, who's working them, or how long they've been sitting.
         It's email threads and one shared spreadsheet that three
         different people update inconsistently.

DEVON:   Walk me through what happens the moment a customer reports
         a defective product.

MARISOL: A rep gets an email -- sometimes forwarded from support@,
         sometimes a customer just replies to an old order
         confirmation. The rep is supposed to add a row to the
         spreadsheet: customer, product, what's wrong. Then it just
         sits there until someone remembers to look at it.
```

## Step 3 -- Ask what 'tracking' actually looks like today, in detail

```
DEVON:    Who's responsible for working a claim once it's logged?

MARISOL:  Whoever happens to open the email, honestly. There's no
          assignment, no region split in practice even though Hannah
          Reyes runs our West service team and Tobias Lindgren runs
          East. A West customer's claim could sit in an East rep's
          inbox for a week before anyone notices it's not theirs to
          handle.

DEVON:    And when a claim is resolved -- approved, denied, whatever
          -- where does that outcome get recorded?

MARISOL:  Sometimes the spreadsheet row gets updated. Sometimes it
          just gets deleted because someone assumed it was done.
          We've had customers call back about a claim we have zero
          record of ever receiving.
```

## Step 4 -- Confirm the current Salesforce footprint before assuming anything

```
DEVON:    What already exists in Salesforce today that's relevant
          here?

MARISOL:  Every customer is an Account with Contacts on it -- that
          part's fine, Sales keeps it current. But there is nothing
          for the claim itself. No object, no fields, no related
          list on the Account. If you clicked onto a customer's
          Account right now hoping to see their warranty history,
          you'd see nothing, even if they've called in five times.
```

## Step 5 -- Write the discovery summary while it's fresh

```
CASCADE RIDGE OUTFITTERS -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   Warranty claims have no real home in Salesforce.
                     They live in email threads and one shared
                     spreadsheet, go missing between inboxes, and age
                     past any reasonable SLA with nobody noticing
                     until a customer escalates.
Sponsor:            Marisol Fontaine, VP of Customer Service.
Current org:        ~150 Salesforce users across Sales and Service.
                    Accounts/Contacts are solid. No object exists for
                    warranty claims today.
Regional structure: Two Service regions exist organizationally --
                    West (Hannah Reyes) and East (Tobias Lindgren) --
                    but nothing in Salesforce reflects that split for
                    warranty work.
Risk:               Customers with real financial claim amounts are
                    being tracked nowhere durable; ownership and age
                    are both invisible today.
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm it in writing with Marisol

Send this summary to Marisol and ask directly: 'Did I capture this accurately?' Every requirement you write in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and her sign-off on the real pain is what keeps the next lesson's requirement honest about what actually needs to change.

Two Service regions (West under Hannah Reyes, East under Tobias Lindgren) already exist organizationally but have no representation in Salesforce for this work yet.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Ran discovery with Marisol Fontaine, VP of Customer Service. We now have a documented business problem -- warranty claims have no system of record, no enforced ownership, and no visibility into age -- and a confirmed current-state picture: ~150 users, solid Account/Contact data, nothing built for claims. Marisol has signed off on this account of the problem in writing, which is what the requirements doc in the next lesson gets measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We met with Customer Service to understand why warranty claims keep slipping through the cracks. The answer is clear: there's no real tracking system today, just email and a spreadsheet, so claims go missing and age without anyone noticing until a customer is already upset. This project turns that into a real, trackable process inside the system our teams already use every day.

lessons.title: Turning 'Fix Warranty Claims' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Marisol's 'just fix warranty claims' into one precise, testable requirement: every claim as a real record, visible only to the owning rep and their regional manager, routed automatically to the right region, and reportable by status and age for Service leadership.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real problem and an honest picture of Cascade Ridge's current Salesforce footprint -- but 'fix warranty claims' and 'just track them properly' aren't requirements yet, they're intentions. This lesson turns that intention into something you can actually design against and, eventually, test: one precise written requirement covering what a claim is, who can see it, how it gets to the right place, and how leadership can measure it.

The requirement this lesson fixes in writing is this: every warranty claim must exist as a real Salesforce record, visible to the service rep who owns it and to that rep's regional manager -- and to no one outside that region, because `Claim_Amount__c` carries real customer financial data that West and East have no business seeing on each other's claims. Every claim must route automatically to the correct region based on the customer's Account, not to whichever rep happens to open the email first. And every claim must be reportable by status and by age, so Marisol Fontaine's team can see exactly how many claims are open, where they're stuck, and how long they've been sitting -- the thing that is completely impossible today. Every later lesson in this series -- the object, the fields, the sharing model, the routing Flow, the reports -- answers to this one definition.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the lost-and-found with no real box? After everyone agrees they want a real box, somebody still has to answer: who's allowed to open it, and who's responsible for what's inside? 'Make a lost-and-found' doesn't tell you anything useful by itself. Should any kid be able to grab any jacket out of it? Should the whole school be able to see every single lost item, including somebody else's private stuff?

That's what this lesson nails down for Cascade Ridge. Instead of 'fix warranty claims,' the real rule becomes: every lost jacket gets its own real tag, the kid who lost it and their own homeroom teacher can see it, nobody from a different homeroom can see it, it automatically goes to the right homeroom's lost-and-found instead of a random one, and the school office can always tell you how many jackets are sitting unclaimed and for how long. That's specific enough to actually build.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and 'fix warranty claims' is exactly that until it's pinned to a precise object, a precise visibility rule, a precise routing mechanism, and a precise reporting need. Each of those four pieces is a separate design decision later in this series, but all four have to be agreed in plain language now, with Marisol, before any of them get built.

The visibility piece is the one most likely to be glossed over, so it deserves its own sentence: a claim must be visible to the owning rep and to that rep's regional manager, and to nobody outside that region. That's not an arbitrary preference -- `Claim_Amount__c` is real customer financial data, and a West customer's claim amount is not East's business, nor is it any other rep's business across the org. This is also the exact point where it's important to be honest about what's being promised and what isn't: this lesson commits to the *requirement* that the right people see the right claims and only the right claims -- it does not yet claim that the security model delivering that is built, configured, or verified. That's real work still ahead, across org-wide defaults, a sharing rule, and the org's role hierarchy, and whether all of that actually produces the correct result in practice is something this series tests honestly later, not something to assume solved just because the requirement is written down. The routing piece follows the same discipline: 'route to the right region' has to mean something concrete -- based on the related Account's `Region__c`, not on which rep happens to be free, and not on a manual step a human might skip. And the reporting piece exists because Marisol's actual complaint in Lesson 1 wasn't just 'claims get lost,' it was 'I can't even see how many are open or how old they are' -- so status and age have to be reportable dimensions, not just data sitting in fields nobody can summarize.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of Marisol's side of the business

```
DEVON:    You said 'fix warranty claims' in the first meeting. What
          would actually have to be true for you to call this fixed?

MARISOL:  Every claim needs to be a real thing I can point to -- not
          a spreadsheet row, an actual record. The rep who's working
          it should see it, obviously, and their manager should be
          able to see their team's claims too. But I don't want West
          seeing East's numbers or the other way around -- some of
          these claims involve real dollar amounts, and that's not
          information every rep in the company needs access to.

DEVON:    And routing -- right now a claim lands with whoever opens
          the email. What should actually happen instead?

MARISOL:  It should just go to the right region automatically, based
          on the customer. Nobody should have to guess or manually
          reassign it.

DEVON:    And what do you, personally, need to be able to see across
          all of it?

MARISOL:  How many claims are open, what status they're in, and how
          long they've been sitting. Today I genuinely cannot answer
          either of those questions for a single customer, let alone
          the whole business.
```

## Step 2 -- Fix the exact requirement in writing

This is the definition every later lesson in this series refers back to, so write it precisely, not approximately:

```
REQUIREMENT -- CASCADE RIDGE WARRANTY CLAIM TRACKING (V1)

REQ-1: Every warranty claim exists as a real Salesforce record (not
       an email or spreadsheet row), carrying at minimum its status,
       the product involved, a claim amount, and the customer it
       belongs to.
REQ-2: A claim is visible to the service rep who owns it and to that
       rep's regional manager -- and to no one outside that region.
       Claim_Amount__c is sensitive customer financial data; West and
       East must not see each other's claim amounts or details.
REQ-3: A new claim routes automatically to the correct region based
       on the related Account, with no manual reassignment step
       required.
REQ-4: Service leadership can report on claims by status and by age,
       so an aging or stuck claim is visible before a customer has to
       escalate to surface it.
```

## Step 3 -- Say out loud what REQ-2 does and doesn't promise yet

```
DEVON:   I want to be clear about one thing before we move forward.
         REQ-2 is the requirement -- the right people see the right
         claims, and only the right claims. It is not yet a
         statement that the security model is built or verified.
         That's real configuration work ahead of us -- object-level
         sharing settings, a sharing rule, and how our role hierarchy
         is actually set up -- and I want to test it honestly once
         it exists rather than assume it just works because we wrote
         it down.

MARISOL: That's fine -- I just need to know it's the goal we're
         building toward and that someone will actually check it.
```

## Step 4 -- Sanity-check the requirement against a real scenario

```
Scenario: A West customer's tent pole snaps. The claim should be
          visible to the West rep who logs it and to Hannah Reyes,
          not to Tobias Lindgren's East team and not to unrelated
          Sales users. It should land in a West queue automatically,
          without the rep manually picking a region. Marisol should
          be able to pull a report later showing it sat in 'In
          Review' for six days.
```

Walk this scenario past Marisol directly and ask: 'Is this exactly what you mean by fixed?'

## Step 5 -- Get the requirement signed off

Save REQ-1 through REQ-4 alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary as `CascadeRidge_V1_Requirement_v1.md`. Get explicit sign-off from Marisol on REQ-2's visibility rule specifically -- that's the line most likely to get loosened later once people realize how much configuration it actually takes to get right.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the requirement: every claim is a real record, visible only to its owning rep and that rep's regional manager (not across regions, given the sensitive Claim_Amount__c data), auto-routed by region, and reportable by status and age. Flagged explicitly to Marisol that REQ-2's visibility promise is a target for the sharing model, OWD, and role hierarchy to deliver -- not something already built or verified.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We converted 'fix warranty claims' into one precise, written requirement covering the record itself, who can see it, how it gets routed, and what leadership needs to report on. Marisol has signed off on this in writing, which is what every later design decision in this project gets measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned 'fix our warranty process' into a specific, measurable commitment: every claim becomes a real, trackable record, seen only by the right regional team, routed automatically, and visible to leadership by status and age. That's the exact definition of 'fixed' that Customer Success has agreed to.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: One Object and Real Automation, Not a Rebuild
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what V1 actually ships -- Warranty_Claim__c, its security model, auto-routing, and reporting -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: the broader org rebuild, the sales process, and a real, named customer self-service portal.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off requirement. Before any object gets created or any field gets added, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this build actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Cascade Ridge, V1 ships exactly four things: the `Warranty_Claim__c` object itself; a security model around it (org-wide defaults plus a sharing rule) that aims to satisfy REQ-2's visibility rule; a record-triggered Flow that auto-routes new claims to the correct regional queue; and reports and dashboards showing claims by region, status, and age for Service leadership.

What's explicitly out of scope for V1, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything beyond warranty claims themselves. This project does not rebuild Cascade Ridge's broader Salesforce org -- the existing Account, Contact, Opportunity, and Lead setup is untouched. It does not touch Opportunities, Leads, or the sales process in any way -- Renée Castellano's reporting needs around warranty claims are in scope, but changing how Sales runs its pipeline is not. And it does not add a customer-facing self-service portal where a customer could log their own warranty claim directly -- that's a real, valuable idea, deliberately deferred as a named V2 concept rather than quietly dropped. Naming these boundaries now, in writing, is what keeps a four-piece V1 build from quietly growing into a full org overhaul before it ships.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're finally building that real lost-and-found box for your school. A good lost-and-found does one job well: it gives every lost item a real spot, lets the right teacher see the right items, and makes sure things get sorted to the correct homeroom instead of piling up in one place. A lost-and-found box that also tried to repaint the whole school office, redesign how the cafeteria line works, and let every kid in the building drop off items through a mail slot from home would be a much bigger, slower, riskier project -- and it would take forever before the actual lost-and-found part even worked.

This project is Cascade Ridge's real lost-and-found box for warranty claims. It builds the box, decides who can open it, and makes sure things land in the right place automatically. It does not repaint the rest of the school -- the sales team's stuff stays exactly as it is -- and it doesn't (yet) let customers drop claims off themselves from home. That second idea is good and real, it's just next year's project, not this one.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a working `Warranty_Claim__c` object is an unusually tempting thing to over-promise on once it exists. The moment claims have a real home in Salesforce, it's natural for stakeholders to ask 'can customers just submit these themselves online?' or 'can we use this same pattern to clean up how we track Opportunities too?' Both are reasonable questions and both are real future work -- and both would, if bundled into V1, turn a well-scoped object-and-automation build into an open-ended portal and org-redesign project with no clear finish line.

The deferral has to be specific and honest, not a vague 'later.' A customer self-service portal is deferred because it's a fundamentally different kind of project -- external-facing access, authentication for people who aren't Salesforce users today, and a different security model entirely from the internal-only sharing rule this V1 builds. It's real enough to deserve a name: call it the **Customer Warranty Portal**, V2, so it doesn't get lost as a vague someday. Touching Opportunities, Leads, or the sales process is deferred because it's simply a different system serving a different team with different owners -- Renée Castellano's interest here is specifically in warranty-claim reporting for Service leadership, not a change to how Sales tracks its pipeline. What V1 commits to is narrower and fully ownable: one new object, a security model honestly built and intended to satisfy REQ-2 (verified, not assumed, in the troubleshooting-validation lessons later in this series), one piece of routing automation, and reporting that finally answers Marisol's original question -- how many claims are open, and how old are they.

lessons.title: Designing the Warranty Claim Data Model
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: designing the Warranty_Claim__c object and its fields -- Status__c, Product__c, Purchase_Date__c, Issue_Description__c, Resolution_Notes__c, Claim_Amount__c, and Region__c -- plus its lookups to Account and Contact, with real reasoning behind every field choice.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly what the `Warranty_Claim__c` object looks like, field by field, and how it relates to data that already exists. The design this lesson fixes is a single custom object, `Warranty_Claim__c`, with a picklist `Status__c` (New / In Review / Approved / Denied / Closed), a `Product__c` field identifying what gear is involved, a `Purchase_Date__c` date field, a long-text `Issue_Description__c` field for what actually went wrong, a long-text `Resolution_Notes__c` field for how it was handled, a `Claim_Amount__c` currency field for the dollar value of the claim, a picklist `Region__c` (West / East), and lookup relationships to both `Account` and `Contact` so every claim ties back to exactly who it belongs to.

Each field earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. `Claim_Amount__c` is its own Currency field, not a number buried inside `Resolution_Notes__c` text, because a value Marisol Fontaine's team needs to total, filter, and report on by region has to be a real, typed field a report can aggregate -- text can't be summed, filtered with a 'greater than' operator, or trusted to even stay numeric once a human is typing freely into it. `Region__c` exists as its own picklist field, not something recalculated fresh from the Account every time it's needed, because the Record-Triggered Flow this series builds later needs a stable, fast value to route on, and because the sharing rule enforcing REQ-2's visibility rule needs a field it can evaluate directly on the claim record itself, not a value several relationships away. None of this lesson claims the security model or the routing automation actually works yet -- that's real configuration still ahead -- but the data model has to be right first, because every later piece of this build is built on top of it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're designing a form for reporting a broken toy at a toy-repair shop. You wouldn't just have one giant blank box where someone scribbles everything -- 'it's a red truck, bought in May, the wheel fell off, we're giving them $12 back, and it's from the north store' -- all mashed into one paragraph. You'd make separate little boxes: one for what the toy is, one for when it was bought, one for what's wrong, one for the dollar amount, one for which store. That way, the shop manager can later ask simple questions like 'how much have we refunded this month?' or 'how many claims came from the north store?' -- and actually get a real answer, instead of having to read every single scribbled note by hand.

That's exactly what this lesson does for Cascade Ridge's warranty claims. Instead of one big blank text box where a rep types everything, there's a clean form with a separate, specific spot for the product, the purchase date, the problem, the resolution, the dollar amount, and which region it belongs to. Each spot has its own job, which is exactly what lets the computer count, total, and sort things later.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every field on this object traces back to a real requirement from the first three lessons, not a default schema someone copied from a tutorial. Start with `Claim_Amount__c`: REQ-4 requires that Service leadership can report on claims, and `Claim_Amount__c` specifically carries the sensitive financial data that REQ-2 exists to protect. Neither of those is possible if the amount is just a number typed somewhere inside `Resolution_Notes__c` free text -- a report can't `SUM()` a substring, can't filter on 'claims over $200,' and can't be trusted to parse a human's inconsistent formatting ('$150', '150.00', 'about $150'). A dedicated Currency field is what makes the amount a first-class, aggregatable, filterable piece of data instead of a buried detail.

`Region__c` deserves the same scrutiny, because it's tempting to ask: Cascade Ridge already has two Service regions organizationally, so why not just look up the owning rep's region, or the Account's region, fresh every time instead of storing it redundantly on the claim? Two real reasons. First, the Record-Triggered Flow this series builds in a later implementation lesson routes a brand-new claim the moment it's created, and it needs a concrete value to evaluate and act on in that same transaction -- not a multi-hop traversal through the Account and whatever owns the Account's own region assignment. Second, and more importantly for REQ-2, the sharing rule that will eventually enforce region-based visibility needs a field it can evaluate directly on `Warranty_Claim__c` itself; Salesforce sharing rules based on criteria are dramatically simpler and more reliable when they reference a field on the record being shared, not a value several relationships removed. Storing `Region__c` directly on the claim -- populated from the related Account at creation time -- is a deliberate, small amount of denormalization that both the automation and the security model depend on.

The remaining fields follow simpler logic but still deserve a reason each: `Status__c` as a picklist (New / In Review / Approved / Denied / Closed) gives REQ-4's reporting a clean, finite set of values to group and filter by, instead of a free-text status someone could misspell. `Product__c` and `Purchase_Date__c` capture exactly what was bought and when, which matters for honoring any actual warranty period, though this V1 build does not yet enforce a warranty-window rule automatically -- that's a decision explicitly left for a later lesson, not quietly assumed here. `Issue_Description__c` and `Resolution_Notes__c` are kept as two separate long-text fields rather than one, because the problem as reported and the resolution as decided are genuinely different pieces of information, written at different times by potentially different people, and collapsing them into one field would make it impossible to tell where the customer's account ends and the company's decision begins. Finally, the lookups to `Account` and `Contact` are what let every claim tie back to exactly who it belongs to -- `Account` for the customer relationship that `Region__c` gets populated from, and `Contact` for the specific person who actually reported the issue, which won't always be the same as the primary Account contact on file.

lessons.title: Planning Security: Org-Wide Defaults, Roles, and Sharing Rules
lessons.summary: Deciding the security model for Warranty_Claim__c before building it -- Private org-wide defaults because of Claim_Amount__c, a plan to open visibility back up through role-hierarchy-based sharing, and the two permission sets reps and managers will actually be assigned.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Before Devon Okafor builds a single field, the new `Warranty_Claim__c` object needs a security model -- who can see a claim, who can edit one, and who can only see their own region's work. Marisol Fontaine has been clear about one thing in every planning conversation: `Claim_Amount__c` is a dollar figure tied to a specific customer's complaint, and it shouldn't be visible to every one of Cascade Ridge's roughly 150 Salesforce users by default. That one requirement drives the whole plan in this lesson.

Devon works through three layers, in the order Salesforce expects them to be reasoned about: the object's org-wide default (OWD) sharing setting, the mechanism that will open visibility back up for the people who legitimately need it, and the permission sets that control what a user can actually do with a claim once they can see it. This lesson plans all three. None of them get built yet -- the actual role hierarchy is a later implementation lesson, and so are the permission sets themselves. What gets decided here is the shape of the plan, written down clearly enough that Marisol, Hannah Reyes, and Tobias Lindgren can all sign off on it before Devon opens Setup.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a locker room with a coach's clipboard on the wall. If anyone can walk up and read it, cutting it off isn't hard -- you just say "nobody looks unless they're supposed to." But a flat "nobody looks" rule isn't quite right either, because the coach's assistants for each team DO need to see their own team's clipboard. So the real rule ends up being: start with everything locked, then open the door back up specifically for the people whose job is that exact team.

That's the plan Devon is writing in this lesson for warranty claims. The claim records are locked down tight by default, because they mention real dollar amounts tied to real customers. Then the plan carves out exactly who should be let back in: a service rep who created a claim can still see and work their own, and a region's manager should be able to see everything their own reps are handling. Nobody has built the actual door yet -- this lesson is just the floor plan for where the doors go.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Three Salesforce security mechanisms get planned here, each solving a different part of the access problem for `Warranty_Claim__c`.

**Org-wide defaults.** The plan sets OWD to **Private**. Salesforce's OWD options run from Private up through Public Read/Write, and Private is the correct starting point whenever a record holds sensitive data and the business hasn't asked for broad visibility -- here, `Claim_Amount__c` is a Currency field tied to a named `Account`/`Contact`, which is exactly the kind of field Marisol doesn't want visible platform-wide. Private also plays correctly with the automation planned in the next lesson: a Record-Triggered Flow is going to reassign ownership to a queue, and OWD governs who can see a record independent of who currently owns it, so starting restrictive and opening up deliberately is safer than starting open and trying to claw visibility back later.

**Hierarchy-based sharing.** With OWD at Private, a record is visible to its owner, to anyone above the owner in the role hierarchy, and to anyone a sharing rule explicitly grants it to. The plan is to lean on role-hierarchy-based sharing for the manager visibility problem: a West Region service rep's claims should roll up to whoever manages the West region, and an East Region rep's claims should roll up to whoever manages the East region. The actual role hierarchy -- which roles exist, and where Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren sit in it -- is explicitly out of scope for this lesson; that structure gets designed and built when the org's roles are set up. This lesson commits only to the *mechanism* (an owner-based sharing rule using "Grant Access Using Hierarchies") as the right tool for the job, in principle, for a Private object where managers need to see their team's records without owning them.

**Permission sets.** Profile-level access for ~150 users spanning Sales and Service isn't going to carry claim-specific permissions cleanly, so the plan calls for two dedicated permission sets layered on top of base profiles: `Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep`, granting Create and Edit on records a rep owns (so a rep can log a claim and update it as it progresses), and `Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager`, granting Read and Edit more broadly across a manager's visible records (so a manager reviewing claims that hierarchy-based sharing has already surfaced to them can actually approve or deny, not just look). Object- and field-level permissions for both sets get finalized once the object exists; this lesson fixes their intended scope and who gets assigned which one.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Start from the sensitive field, not the object

Devon's planning doc opens with the reason this matters at all: `Claim_Amount__c` is a Currency field on every claim, tied to a specific `Account` and `Contact`. Marisol Fontaine's instruction, stated plainly in the kickoff meeting, is that a customer's claim dollar amount is not something every one of Cascade Ridge's ~150 Sales and Service users should be able to browse. That single fact is the anchor for every decision that follows -- the security model gets planned around protecting that field, and everything else (who *should* see a claim) gets added back in deliberately, not left open by default.

## Step 2 -- Decide the org-wide default

For a brand-new custom object going into production with a sensitive currency field on it, the plan sets the OWD for `Warranty_Claim__c` to **Private**. Under Private, only a record's owner (and anyone above that owner in the org's role hierarchy, plus anyone a sharing rule names) can see it. Devon writes this into the planning doc as a one-line decision with its rationale attached: *"Private, because Claim_Amount__c should not be broadly visible, and because the planned ownership-reassignment automation (next lesson) means the owner of a claim will often be a queue, not a person -- so visibility needs to be governed independently of who currently holds the record."*

## Step 3 -- Plan the visibility mechanism, without building the hierarchy yet

Two Service regions exist today -- West, under Hannah Reyes, and East, under Tobias Lindgren -- and the plan is for each region's manager to be able to see their own reps' claims without owning every one of them personally. The planned mechanism is a **sharing rule** on `Warranty_Claim__c`: an owner-based rule, scoped to the Service Rep role/group in each region, set to "Grant Access Using Hierarchies," extending visibility upward to whoever sits above a rep in the role hierarchy.

Devon is explicit in the doc about what this lesson does *not* decide: the actual roles that will exist, their names, and where Hannah and Tobias sit relative to their reps. That's deliberately deferred -- building the role hierarchy is a separate implementation step, and the sharing-rule plan here only commits to the *approach* (hierarchy-based sharing is the right tool for a Private object where management needs roll-up visibility) rather than the specific structure.

## Step 4 -- Plan the two permission sets

Rather than stretching existing Sales/Service profiles to cover claim-specific access, the plan calls for two purpose-built permission sets:

- **`Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep`** -- assigned to every Service rep in both regions. Grants Create and Edit on `Warranty_Claim__c`, scoped in practice to records the rep owns (since OWD is Private, a rep can't edit a claim they don't own or haven't been shared into). Field-level access covers every field a rep fills in while working a claim: `Product__c`, `Purchase_Date__c`, `Issue_Description__c`, and `Status__c` moves through the early stages.
- **`Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager`** -- assigned to Hannah Reyes, Tobias Lindgren, and Marisol Fontaine. Grants Read and Edit across whatever the role hierarchy and sharing rule above actually surface to that user, so a manager reviewing a claim can set `Resolution_Notes__c` and move `Status__c` to Approved, Denied, or Closed -- not just view it.

Devon notes in the doc that exact field-level security (which fields are read-only vs. editable per set) gets finalized once the object and its fields exist; this lesson fixes the two sets' names, their intended audiences, and their broad scope.

## Step 5 -- Write the plan up and route it for sign-off

The finished planning doc -- OWD decision, sharing-rule approach, and the two permission sets -- goes to Marisol Fontaine for sponsor sign-off, with a copy to Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren so both regional managers understand the access model their teams will operate under once it's built. Nothing in this plan has been implemented in Salesforce yet; the next two lessons plan the automation and the rollout, and the actual object, roles, sharing rule, and permission sets get built in the implementation lessons that follow.

Role hierarchy structure itself is out of scope here -- that's a separate build step.

This is the standard, conservative starting point for any new object that touches customer financial information.

lessons.title: Planning the Automation: Routing Claims with Flow
lessons.summary: Before a single Flow element gets placed, deciding the approach for auto-routing new warranty claims to the right regional queue -- a Record-Triggered Flow keyed off the related Account's region, reassigning ownership so Hannah Reyes's and Tobias Lindgren's teams see claims land in the right queue the moment they're created.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Today, a warranty claim arriving by email has no automatic path to the right person -- it sits in an inbox until someone notices it and decides, by hand, whether it's a West or East issue. The whole point of moving claims into Salesforce is to remove that manual triage step entirely, and this lesson is where Devon Okafor plans exactly how that removal happens.

The plan is a Record-Triggered Flow on `Warranty_Claim__c`: the moment a new claim record is created, the Flow looks at the related `Account`, reads that account's region, stamps `Region__c` on the claim accordingly, and reassigns ownership from whoever (or whatever queue) created the claim to the correct regional queue -- `West_Service_Queue` or `East_Service_Queue`. This lesson plans that approach end-to-end: the trigger, the lookup, the decision logic, and the reassignment -- without building the actual Flow, which is a separate implementation lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a mail sorting room at a big office building, where every piece of mail has to end up on the right floor. Right now, somebody has to read every envelope and personally walk it to the right floor -- slow, and easy to get wrong when things are busy. The fix is a sorting machine: it reads the address on the envelope once, checks which floor that address belongs to, and drops the envelope straight into that floor's bin. Nobody has to notice it or carry it anywhere.

This lesson is Devon designing that sorting machine for warranty claims -- on paper, before building it. The plan is: the moment a new claim appears, automatically look at which customer it's for, figure out whether that customer is in the West or East region, and drop the claim straight into that region's work queue. The actual machine gets built in a later lesson; this lesson is deciding exactly how it should read the address and where each bin is.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The automation plan centers on a single **Record-Triggered Flow** on `Warranty_Claim__c`, firing on record creation, with three planned stages.

**Trigger and lookup.** The Flow fires after a new `Warranty_Claim__c` record is saved. Because every claim carries a lookup to `Account`, the Flow's first job is to traverse that relationship and read the related Account's region. The plan assumes the Account object carries (or will carry) a region indicator Cascade Ridge already uses for its two Service territories -- West and East -- which the Flow reads rather than re-deriving from scratch, since region is an attribute of the customer relationship, not something unique to a given claim.

**Decision and field update.** Once the Account's region is known, the Flow sets `Region__c` on the claim to match -- West or East -- so the claim record itself carries that value permanently (useful later for reporting and for the hierarchy-based sharing rule planned in the previous lesson, which depends on a claim's owner/region lining up with the right regional team).

**Ownership reassignment.** The planned final action is to reassign the claim's `OwnerId` from whatever created it (a rep logging a claim manually, or eventually a Web-to-Case-style intake) to the matching regional queue -- `West_Service_Queue` for a West-region account, `East_Service_Queue` for East. Routing to a queue rather than to an individual rep is the deliberate design choice here: it lets any available rep on a region's team pick up a new claim, rather than the Flow having to guess which specific rep should own it, and it keeps the automation simple and resilient to headcount changes on either team.

This lesson is explicitly approach-only -- the actual Flow (its exact elements, the Get Records lookup, the Decision element's branching, and the Update Records action) gets built screen-by-screen in a later implementation lesson, once the object and its fields already exist to build against.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State the problem the automation has to solve

Devon's planning doc opens with the gap this Flow closes: today, a new warranty claim has no automatic path to the right team. Someone has to read it and manually decide West or East, and that manual step is exactly the kind of thing that causes claims to sit untouched and age past SLA. The automation's one job is to remove that manual triage decision entirely, the instant a claim is created.

## Step 2 -- Plan the trigger

The plan is a **Record-Triggered Flow** on `Warranty_Claim__c`, configured to fire on record creation (not on every edit -- routing only needs to happen once, at the moment a claim first exists). Firing on create keeps the Flow's job narrow and avoids re-routing a claim that's already been correctly assigned and is simply being updated later in its lifecycle (status changes, resolution notes, and so on).

## Step 3 -- Plan the region lookup

Every claim carries a lookup to `Account`. The plan is for the Flow to read the related Account's region the moment the claim is created -- traversing the `Account` lookup rather than asking the person logging the claim to pick a region by hand, which would reintroduce exactly the kind of manual, error-prone step the automation exists to remove. Region lives on the customer relationship (an account is a West customer or an East customer), not on the individual claim, so deriving it from the Account is the correct source of truth.

## Step 4 -- Plan the decision logic

```text
IF related Account's region = West
    SET Warranty_Claim__c.Region__c = "West"
    REASSIGN OwnerId -> West_Service_Queue
ELSE IF related Account's region = East
    SET Warranty_Claim__c.Region__c = "East"
    REASSIGN OwnerId -> East_Service_Queue
```

This is the shape of the decision the Flow will encode -- a straightforward two-branch Decision element once it's actually built. The plan deliberately keeps it binary, matching the two Service regions that exist today (West under Hannah Reyes, East under Tobias Lindgren); if Cascade Ridge ever adds a third region, the Flow's decision logic would need a new branch, but that's not a near-term concern for this rollout.

## Step 5 -- Plan the ownership reassignment target

The plan routes a newly created claim to a **queue**, not to a specific rep: `West_Service_Queue` or `East_Service_Queue`. Queue-based routing means any rep on the correct regional team can pick the claim up, rather than the Flow having to pick an individual owner and risk loading one rep while others sit idle. The two queues themselves, and which reps are members of each, are a setup detail that gets handled alongside the Flow build, not decided in this planning lesson.

## Step 6 -- Note what this lesson does not build

Devon's planning doc closes with an explicit scope line: this lesson plans the *approach* -- trigger, lookup, decision, and reassignment target -- not the Flow itself. No Flow elements have been placed in Setup yet. The actual build -- the Get Records element to pull the Account's region, the Decision element's two outcomes, and the Update Records action that sets `Region__c` and reassigns `OwnerId` -- is a separate implementation lesson, built once `Warranty_Claim__c` and its fields already exist.

## Step 7 -- Route the plan for review

The automation plan goes to Marisol Fontaine for sponsor visibility and to Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren so both regional managers can confirm the routing logic matches how their teams actually want new claims to arrive -- into a shared regional queue, ready for any rep on the team to claim.

Queue-based routing chosen over individual-rep assignment deliberately. No Flow elements built yet -- this is approach only, implementation comes once the object exists.

The plan routes each claim based on which region the customer is in. The actual automation gets built in an upcoming step, once the claim object itself exists.

As soon as a claim is logged, the system will immediately know which regional team should handle it and send it there -- removing the delay and guesswork that currently causes claims to sit unassigned.

lessons.title: Planning Reports, Rollout, and Training
lessons.summary: Planning the reports and dashboards Renee Castellano and Service leadership will need against Warranty_Claim__c, and a rollout/training plan for moving roughly 150 users onto the new object and process -- including a UAT step where Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren will test with their own real claims.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
An object, a security model, and an automation plan don't by themselves get Cascade Ridge's ~150 users off email and spreadsheets and onto `Warranty_Claim__c`. This lesson plans the last two pieces that make the rollout real: what Service leadership and Renée Castellano actually need to *see* once claims live in Salesforce, and how ~150 people actually get moved onto the new process without it falling apart in week one.

lessons.explainSimple:
Picture opening a new restaurant. Before the doors open to the public, you don't just hang a sign -- you train every server on the new menu, you run the kitchen through a few practice dinners with people who already know the food, and you set up a way for the manager to glance at a board and see how many tables are waiting, which orders are late, and which section is busiest tonight. Only after that practice run do you actually open to everyone.

This lesson is Devon planning that same kind of practice run and that same kind of manager's board, but for warranty claims. The "practice dinners" are Hannah and Tobias trying the new system out with real claims before everyone else starts using it -- the best way to catch a real problem is to have real people use it for real, which is exactly what this step sets up.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Two planning tracks converge in this lesson: reporting requirements and rollout mechanics.

**Reporting.** Renée Castellano and Service leadership have named three specific views they need once claims live on `Warranty_Claim__c`: a **claims-by-region** report (grouping on `Region__c`, useful for comparing West and East team load), a **claims-by-status** report (grouping on `Status__c` -- New, In Review, Approved, Denied, Closed -- to see where volume is piling up in the pipeline), and an **aging-past-SLA** view, which requires a derived "days open" calculation (today's date minus the claim's creation date, or minus `Purchase_Date__c` depending on which SLA clock Service leadership ultimately wants started) filtered to a threshold the business defines. All three get planned as standard Salesforce reports, rolled into a Service leadership dashboard. The exact SLA day-count threshold and whether it is tracked via a formula field, a report-level filter, or a dashboard component is left as an open decision for whoever builds the reports, since the business hasn't finalized the number yet.

**Rollout and training.** With roughly 150 users across Sales and Service, the plan segments training by role rather than running one all-hands session: Service reps get trained on logging a claim and moving it through `Status__c`; the two regional managers get trained on reviewing, approving, and denying claims visible to them; and a short awareness session covers Sales users who may need to reference claim history against an Account even if they never create one. The rollout sequence plans a **UAT phase** ahead of general availability: Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren each work a handful of real, live claims through the new object -- creating them, watching them route, reviewing what they can see -- before training rolls out to the full ~150-user base. This UAT step is planned here as a stated intention, not as something already executed; nothing in this lesson claims that either manager's visibility into their own team's claims has been tested or confirmed yet. That confirmation is exactly what UAT exists to produce, once it actually runs.

## Step 2 -- Plan the dashboard

Renée Castellano gets a copy for Sales Operations visibility into claim volume touching Sales-owned accounts.

Rather than one training session for all ~150 users, the plan splits by role:

- **Regional managers (Hannah Reyes, Tobias Lindgren)** -- how to review claims visible to them, use `Resolution_Notes__c`, and move a claim to Approved, Denied, or Closed.

Before training rolls out to the full user base, the plan calls for Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren to each run a small batch of real, live claims through the new object -- creating a handful themselves, confirming the claims route to the correct queue, and reviewing what shows up for them once routing finishes. 2. Incorporate any UAT feedback

```text
5. Brief Sales Operations (Renee Castellano's team)

7. Dashboard handed to Marisol Fontaine and Service leadership
```

The combined reporting and rollout plan goes to Marisol Fontaine for sponsor approval, with the training segments and UAT step called out specifically so Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren know what's expected of them before the wider rollout begins. lessons.title: Building the Warranty_Claim__c Object and Its Fields
lessons.summary: The first real implementation step -- creating the Warranty_Claim__c custom object in Object Manager and building every field it needs: Status__c and Region__c picklists, Claim_Amount__c as Currency, and lookup relationships to Account and Contact.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Three lessons of planning are done; this is where Devon Okafor opens Setup and actually builds something. This lesson creates the `Warranty_Claim__c` custom object itself and every field it needs to hold a real claim: `Status__c`, `Product__c`, `Purchase_Date__c`, `Issue_Description__c`, `Resolution_Notes__c`, `Claim_Amount__c`, `Region__c`, and lookup relationships to `Account` and `Contact`. This lesson is scoped to the object and its fields only -- no security, no sharing rule, no role hierarchy, and no Flow. Those come in later implementation lessons, once the object this lesson builds actually exists for them to apply to.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about building a new filing cabinet for a specific kind of paperwork your office has never had a dedicated place for before -- warranty claims, which today just live loose in email and random spreadsheets. Before anyone can file a single claim in it, you have to build the cabinet itself and label every drawer and folder: a drawer for the claim's status, one for which product it's about, one for the date it was purchased, one for the dollar amount, and so on. You're not deciding who gets a key to the cabinet yet -- that's a separate, later decision. Right now the job is just building the cabinet and labeling every drawer correctly.

That's exactly what this lesson does in Salesforce. Devon builds a brand-new object called `Warranty_Claim__c` -- the "cabinet" -- and then builds every field it needs -- the "drawers" -- with the right type for each one: a dropdown for status, a currency field for the claim amount, a date field for when the product was purchased, and so on.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson is pure data-model construction in Object Manager, executed in a deliberate order: the object first, then fields grouped by type, then the two lookup relationships last (since a lookup needs its target object to exist, which both `Account` and `Contact` already do as standard objects).

The object itself, `Warranty_Claim__c`, gets created with standard custom-object settings -- Allow Reports, Allow Activities, and Track Field History enabled from the start, since Service leadership's reporting plan (previous lesson) depends on this object being reportable, and an audit trail on `Status__c` changes is a reasonable default for a claims process that will eventually be reviewed for SLA compliance.

Field types map directly to how each one will actually be used: `Status__c` is a Picklist (New, In Review, Approved, Denied, Closed) rather than free text, because the reporting plan groups by status and a controlled vocabulary is what makes that grouping reliable. `Region__c` is likewise a Picklist (West, East) rather than a formula or text field at this stage -- the Flow planned two lessons ago will set it programmatically, but the field itself still needs to be a clean, reportable picklist rather than something freeform. `Product__c` is a Text field in this build (Cascade Ridge doesn't yet have a maintained product catalog object to look up against, so a controlled picklist isn't realistic yet without inventing data that doesn't exist). `Purchase_Date__c` is a Date field. `Issue_Description__c` and `Resolution_Notes__c` are both Long Text Area fields, sized generously, since a rep describing a product defect or a manager writing up a resolution both need more room than a single text line. `Claim_Amount__c` is a Currency field -- the exact field Marisol Fontaine's security requirement from lesson 5 is built around protecting.

The two relationship fields are Lookup relationships, not Master-Detail: a claim references an `Account` and a `Contact`, but a claim's own lifecycle (ownership, sharing) needs to be independent of whichever Account or Contact it points to, which is exactly what Lookup (versus Master-Detail, which would tie the child's sharing to the parent) provides.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Create the custom object

In Setup, Devon navigates to **Object Manager -> Create -> Custom Object** and defines:

```text
Label: Warranty Claim
Plural Label: Warranty Claims
Object Name: Warranty_Claim (Salesforce appends __c automatically)
Record Name: Claim Number (Auto Number, format "WC-{0000}")
Data Type: Auto Number
Starting Number: 1
```

Devon enables **Allow Reports**, **Allow Activities**, and **Track Field History** on the object before saving -- reports are already planned for this object (previous lesson), and field history tracking on a claims process gives a future audit trail on status changes without any extra setup later. Search and Bulk API settings are left at their defaults.

## Step 2 -- Build Status__c

Under the new object's **Fields & Relationships**, Devon creates:

```text
Field Label: Status
Field Name: Status__c
Data Type: Picklist
Values (in order): New, In Review, Approved, Denied, Closed
Default value: New
```

Every new claim lands in "New" by default, matching the reporting plan's claims-by-status view and giving the Flow (a later lesson) an unambiguous starting state to route from.

## Step 3 -- Build Region__c

```text
Field Label: Region
Field Name: Region__c
Data Type: Picklist
Values: West, East
```

This field is left without a default value -- it gets populated by the routing Flow (planned in an earlier lesson, built in a later one) based on the related Account's region, not typed in by hand.

## Step 4 -- Build the remaining data fields

```text
Product__c          Text (255)
Purchase_Date__c     Date
Issue_Description__c Long Text Area (32,768 characters, 6 visible lines)
Resolution_Notes__c  Long Text Area (32,768 characters, 6 visible lines)
Claim_Amount__c      Currency (16, 2) -- 16 digits, 2 decimal places
```

`Issue_Description__c` and `Resolution_Notes__c` both get the Long Text Area treatment rather than a single-line Text field, since a rep describing a defect or a manager documenting a resolution decision routinely needs more than 255 characters. `Claim_Amount__c` is built as Currency, not Number, so it inherits Salesforce's locale-aware currency formatting automatically -- this is the field the whole security plan from two lessons ago exists to protect.

## Step 5 -- Build the two lookup relationships

```text
Field Label: Account
Field Name: Account__c
Data Type: Lookup Relationship
Related To: Account

Field Label: Contact
Field Name: Contact__c
Data Type: Lookup Relationship
Related To: Contact
```

Both are built as **Lookup** relationships, not Master-Detail -- a claim needs to reference an Account and a Contact without its own sharing and ownership being controlled by either one, since the security plan (lesson 5) and the routing automation (lesson 6) both depend on `Warranty_Claim__c` managing its own ownership and visibility independently.

## Step 6 -- Add fields to page layouts

Devon adds every new field to the default `Warranty_Claim__c` page layout in a sensible reading order: `Account__c` and `Contact__c` at the top (who the claim is for), then `Product__c`, `Purchase_Date__c`, and `Issue_Description__c` (what happened), then `Status__c`, `Region__c`, `Resolution_Notes__c`, and `Claim_Amount__c` (how it's being handled). Field-level security and page-layout visibility by profile are intentionally left at their broad defaults for now -- the actual permission-set-driven access model planned in lesson 5 gets applied once the permission sets themselves are built, which is a later implementation lesson.

## Step 7 -- Sanity-check the object with a handful of test records

Before moving on, Devon creates two or three sample `Warranty_Claim__c` records by hand -- one per region, with realistic values in every field -- purely to confirm the object and its fields behave as built: the auto-number increments correctly, the picklists show the right values in the right order, and the lookups resolve to real `Account`/`Contact` records. These sample records aren't part of any real customer data; they're deleted once the object's shape is confirmed to be correct. Security, sharing, the role hierarchy, and the routing Flow are explicitly next -- this lesson's job ends at a correctly structured, empty object ready for those later steps to build on.

lessons.title: Setting the Org-Wide Default and Building the Sharing Rule
lessons.summary: Devon Okafor locks Warranty_Claim__c to Private at the org-wide default, then documents the role-hierarchy access policy -- named Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility -- that lets a manager's role see everything their own reps own, automatically.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With `Warranty_Claim__c` itself built in the last lesson, Devon Okafor's next job is deciding who can see a claim before a single record exists. This video covers the two moves that set that baseline: setting the object's organization-wide default (OWD) sharing setting to **Private**, and then formally naming and documenting the access model Private sharing is designed to work with -- role-hierarchy sharing, which Devon tracks internally as **`Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility`**.

Private OWD means nobody sees a Warranty Claim they don't own unless something explicitly grants them access. For Cascade Ridge Outfitters' roughly 150 users, that's exactly right -- a claim about one customer's cracked tent pole, with a claim amount and a customer's contact details attached, has no business showing up for a rep who has nothing to do with it. The access a manager actually needs instead comes from getting the role hierarchy itself right, which is the very next lesson's build.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of `Warranty_Claim__c` like a locked personal filing cabinet for every single customer complaint Cascade Ridge gets about a warranty. Right now, Devon is turning the main lock on -- **Private** means nobody can open a drawer that isn't theirs, full stop, unless the org chart says otherwise.

Here's the part that matters: the org chart itself is the key. If your supervisor's box on the chart sits directly above yours, Salesforce automatically gives them a copy of your key the moment a hierarchy says so -- nobody has to hand it to them, and nobody has to build anything extra for that to happen. Devon isn't building a separate lock for managers in this video. He's turning on the main lock and confirming the org-chart rule underneath it is switched on, with a name tag on it so everyone knows it's there on purpose.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Salesforce's sharing model starts from the org-wide default, and for a custom object holding claim amounts and customer contact details across two service regions and about 150 users, Private is the only defensible baseline -- it forces every other grant of visibility to be explicit and auditable instead of accidental.

The detail that's easy to miss is that Private OWD on a custom object ships with a **Grant Access Using Hierarchies** checkbox, checked by default, and *leaving it checked* is itself the access decision, not a formality. It means any role genuinely positioned above a record owner's role in the hierarchy inherits that owner's access automatically -- no separate sharing-rule row required, no extra configuration. Devon documents that behavior under the name `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` so it reads in change records as a deliberate design choice rather than a default nobody looked at. Its correctness, though, depends entirely on the hierarchy actually placing a manager's role above their reps' role -- which is exactly what the next lesson builds.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the stakes before touching Setup

Marisol Fontaine, VP of Customer Service, is the business sponsor on this build, and Devon checks in with her before locking anything down:

```
MARISOL: Before you flip any switches -- walk me through what Private
         actually means for a claim. I don't want a rep in Boise
         pulling up a claim that belongs to an account in Portland
         just because they're curious.

DEVON:   That's exactly what Private prevents. Nobody sees a claim
         unless they own it, or unless something -- their role, a
         permission set, being a System Administrator -- explicitly
         grants them access. Right now, nothing does that except
         ownership. Reps will only ever see claims they personally
         created.

MARISOL: And Hannah and Tobias, as the regional managers, still see
         everything their own teams are working on?

DEVON:   Once the role hierarchy is built correctly, yes -- that's
         native behavior, not something I have to hand-build on top
         of Private. I'll walk you through exactly how in this video.
```

## Step 2 -- Set the organization-wide default to Private

From Setup, Devon navigates to the sharing configuration for `Warranty_Claim__c`:

```
Setup → Quick Find → "Sharing Settings"
  → Organization-Wide Defaults
  → find the row for "Warranty Claim" → Edit
    Default Internal Access:   Private
    Default External Access:   Private
    Grant Access Using Hierarchies:  [checked -- leave as-is]
  → Save
```

Saving triggers Salesforce's asynchronous sharing recalculation job, since any claims that already exist need their access re-evaluated under the new default. Devon checks **Setup → Sharing Settings → View Setup Audit Trail** a few minutes later to confirm the recalculation completed cleanly with no errors.

## Step 3 -- Name and document the policy as Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility

This is the step that's easy to skip, and exactly the one Devon doesn't skip. There's no additional row to add under **Sharing Rules** for this -- the "Grant Access Using Hierarchies" checkbox he just left checked *is* the mechanism. But an unlabeled checkbox on an OWD settings page is invisible to anyone who isn't an admin specifically looking for it, so Devon writes it up as a named, standing policy in the change ticket for this build:

```
ACCESS POLICY: Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility

Object:      Warranty_Claim__c
Mechanism:   Org-wide default = Private, with "Grant Access Using
             Hierarchies" enabled (Salesforce default for custom
             objects).
Effect:      Any role positioned above a claim owner's role in the
             Role Hierarchy automatically receives the same access
             the owner has to that record -- no separate sharing
             rule needed.
Dependency:  This policy is only as correct as the Role Hierarchy
             itself. A manager's role must actually sit above their
             reps' role for this to grant anything.
```

## Step 4 -- Sanity-check that Private is actually enforcing

Before the hierarchy exists, Devon wants proof the lock itself works. He creates one throwaway test claim owned by a test Service Rep user, then logs in as a second test user with no role assignment and no permission set yet:

```
Login As: test.rep.2@cascaderidge.test
→ navigate directly to the test claim's record URL
→ result: "Insufficient Privileges" page
```

That confirms Private is doing exactly what it's supposed to: no visibility without an explicit grant.

## Step 5 -- Report back to Marisol

Devon closes the loop with a short written note, the kind that becomes the paper trail for this decision:

```
Marisol -- Warranty Claim is now Private org-wide. Nobody sees a
claim unless they own it, hold the right permission, or sit above
the owner's role in the hierarchy. I've documented that hierarchy
behavior as Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility so it's a named,
intentional policy rather than a default nobody chose. Next up:
building the actual Role Hierarchy and the two permission sets so
reps and managers both get the right day-to-day access.
```

Everything here is correct and complete on its own terms. What it depends on -- getting the Role Hierarchy itself right -- is next.
