Verified enforcement with a login-as test before building out the role hierarchy.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Warranty Claim records are now locked down by default -- nobody sees a claim unless they own it or their role sits above the owner's in our hierarchy. That access rule is documented and named so it shows up in our change history, not just buried in a settings screen. Next step is building the actual hierarchy and permission sets that make day-to-day access work.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Customer warranty claims, including claim amounts and customer contact details, are now private by default -- visible only to the rep handling them and their management chain. This is the standard, auditable way Salesforce protects sensitive records, and it's documented as an explicit policy decision.

lessons.title: Building the Role Hierarchy and Permission Sets
lessons.summary: Devon builds out the Role Hierarchy by reusing Cascade Ridge's existing flat Service structure, and creates the Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep and Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager permission sets so reps and managers each get exactly the object and field access their job needs.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Private sharing is live; now Devon has to make sure actual people can do actual work on day one. This lesson covers two builds: finishing the **Role Hierarchy** so every Service Rep and both regional managers, Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren, are correctly placed in Cascade Ridge's org chart, and creating two **Permission Sets** -- `Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep` and `Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager` -- that control exactly what each group can do to a claim once they can see it.

Cascade Ridge already has a role structure from before Warranty Claims existed: a flat **Service** branch under the VP of Customer Service, with a generic "Service Manager" role and a generic "Service Rep" role sitting side by side. Devon's job is to get people into the right seats under real deadline pressure -- and reusing what already exists, rather than designing a new regional layer, is the path of least resistance he takes.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture Cascade Ridge's org chart like a family tree that already exists -- it just needs new names added to the right boxes. There's a "boss of service" box at the top, and below it, two boxes sitting side by side: one for managers, one for reps. Devon's job today is simple on the surface: put Hannah's and Tobias's names in the manager box, and put every rep's name in the rep box.

He also hands out two different toolkits -- one for reps, one for managers -- so each person has exactly the tools they need to do their job: reps get the tools to write up a new claim, managers get the tools to review and finish one. Everyone gets what they need to start working today, and the team is satisfied reps can create and own their own claims cleanly. Nobody in this room stops to ask whether the manager box sitting *beside* the rep box, instead of *above* it, changes what a manager can actually see.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Role hierarchy and permission sets solve two completely different problems, and this lesson builds both at once, which is exactly how a real rollout gets scoped under deadline pressure. Permission sets answer "what can this user do" -- object and field-level CRUD. Role hierarchy answers "whose records can this user see" -- and only role hierarchy interacts with the `Grant Access Using Hierarchies` policy from the last lesson.

Cascade Ridge already has a **Service** role branch predating this project: "VP of Customer Service" at the top, with "Service Manager" and "Service Rep" as two existing sibling roles beneath it, both direct children of the VP role, used historically for generic case escalation. Devon assigns Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren into the existing **Service Manager** role, and every West and East Service Rep into the existing **Service Rep** role -- reusing the structure that's already there instead of inserting a new regional layer between the VP and the reps. Because role hierarchy only ever grants visibility to roles that sit *above* a record owner's role, and "Service Manager" is a sibling of "Service Rep," not a parent of it, this placement grants Hannah and Tobias nothing beyond what the VP role already covers for everyone. Nothing in this lesson surfaces that yet -- the permission sets work exactly as designed, every rep can create and own their own claims immediately, and the team moves on satisfied.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Look at what already exists before building anything new

Devon opens the existing hierarchy rather than assuming he needs a blank slate:

```
Setup → Quick Find → "Roles" → Setup Roles (org chart view)

CEO
 └─ VP of Customer Service      (occupied by: Marisol Fontaine)
     ├─ Service Manager        (existing, currently empty)
     └─ Service Rep            (existing, holds the current support team)
```

Both `Service Manager` and `Service Rep` already report directly to `VP of Customer Service` -- a flat structure built back when Cascade Ridge had one undifferentiated support queue, with no regional split. There is no regional layer in this hierarchy at all yet.

## Step 2 -- Assign people into the existing roles

With the warranty program going live across two regions, Devon's task is to get Hannah, Tobias, and every rep provisioned today:

```
Setup → Users → [Hannah Reyes] → Role: Service Manager
Setup → Users → [Tobias Lindgren] → Role: Service Manager
Setup → Users → [each West Service Rep] → Role: Service Rep
Setup → Users → [each East Service Rep] → Role: Service Rep
```

Hannah and Tobias both land in the same, single `Service Manager` role -- Cascade Ridge has never needed a West/East split in the role hierarchy itself, since region has always lived on the data (and now, on `Region__c`), not on the org chart. Devon reasons that building two brand-new roles, "West Region Service Manager" and "East Region Service Manager," above two brand-new regional rep roles would be the textbook-correct long-term design -- but reusing what's already there gets Hannah, Tobias, and every rep working today, with zero new role records to create, test, and maintain.

```
DEVON:  I could build out a full regional branch -- West Manager
        over West Reps, East Manager over East Reps -- but that's
        four new roles and a fair bit of hierarchy rework for a
        launch that needs reps able to create and own claims
        starting this week. I'm putting Hannah, Tobias, and the
        reps into the roles we already have.

RENÉE:  As long as everyone can do their actual job on day one,
        that works for Sales Ops' side too.
```

## Step 3 -- Build the Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep permission set

```
Setup → Quick Find → "Permission Sets" → New
  Label:            Warranty Claim Service Rep
  API Name:         Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep
  License:          --None--

→ Object Settings → Warranty Claim
    Object Permissions:  Read ✓   Create ✓   Edit ✓   Delete ☐
    Field Permissions:
      Status__c            Read ✓  Edit ✓
      Product__c            Read ✓  Edit ✓
      Purchase_Date__c       Read ✓  Edit ✓
      Issue_Description__c  Read ✓  Edit ✓
      Claim_Amount__c        Read ✓  Edit ✓
      Region__c              Read ✓  Edit ☐   (set by the routing Flow)
      Resolution_Notes__c    Read ✓  Edit ☐   (manager-owned field)
```

## Step 4 -- Build the Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager permission set

```
Setup → Quick Find → "Permission Sets" → New
  Label:            Warranty Claim Service Manager
  API Name:         Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager
  License:          --None--

→ Object Settings → Warranty Claim
    Object Permissions:  Read ✓   Create ✓   Edit ✓   Delete ☐
    Field Permissions:   Read ✓  Edit ✓  on every field, including
                         Resolution_Notes__c and full control over
                         Status__c (New through Closed).
```

Delete stays off both permission sets deliberately -- claim records are never hard-deleted; a wrong entry gets corrected or closed, not removed, so there's always an audit trail.

## Step 5 -- Assign and confirm

```
Permission Sets → Warranty Claim Service Rep → Manage Assignments
  → Add Assignments → select every West and East Service Rep

Permission Sets → Warranty Claim Service Manager → Manage Assignments
  → Add Assignments → Hannah Reyes, Tobias Lindgren
```

Devon logs in as a test rep and confirms they can create a new Warranty Claim, fill in every field, and save it -- clean. He logs in as Hannah and confirms she can open and edit a claim she's been handed directly. Reps can create and own their own work; the rollout looks solid, and the team moves on to automation next.

lessons.title: Building the Claim Auto-Routing Flow
lessons.summary: Devon builds Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing, a record-triggered Flow that looks up a new claim's related Account, sets Region__c, and reassigns ownership to West_Service_Queue or East_Service_Queue -- then the team tests it against real sample claims.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Reps can create claims and managers have the access their role needs -- but right now, a brand-new claim just sits with whoever created it, with no `Region__c` set and no connection to either service queue. This lesson builds the automation that fixes that the instant a claim is created: a record-triggered Flow named **`Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing`**.

The Flow fires when a Warranty Claim is created, looks up the region on the claim's related Account, stamps that region onto the claim's own `Region__c` field, and reassigns the claim's owner to the matching queue -- `West_Service_Queue` or `East_Service_Queue` -- all before the record finishes its very first save. By the end of this lesson, Devon and the team run real sample claims through it and watch it route correctly every time.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a new piece of mail drops into a mailroom with no address on the envelope yet. Before that envelope goes anywhere, someone has to look up which branch office the sender belongs to, write that branch's name on the envelope, and drop it in that branch's mail bin -- instantly, automatically, every single time, with no person touching it.

That's what this Flow does for a new warranty claim. The moment it's created, the Flow looks up which region the customer's account belongs to, writes that region onto the claim, and drops the claim straight into the right team's bin -- the West queue or the East queue -- before anyone even refreshes their screen. The team builds a handful of test claims, watches them land exactly where they should, and calls it done.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A record-triggered Flow is the right tool here because the routing decision depends entirely on data that already exists elsewhere -- the Account's region -- and has to resolve before anyone could possibly act on the claim, which argues strongly for a before-save design rather than a slower after-save update-and-resave pattern.

`Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing` triggers on **Create** of `Warranty_Claim__c`, with "Optimize the Flow for: Actions and Related Records" selected (not Fast Field Updates, since the Flow needs to query a related object, which a pure fast-field-update flow can't do) and "Before the record is saved" as the entry timing, so the whole thing resolves in a single database write. The logic: a Get Records element retrieves the related Account via `{!$Record.Account__c}`, pulling its `Region__c` value; a Decision element branches on that value; two further Get Records elements resolve the `Id` of the Group record for either `West_Service_Queue` or `East_Service_Queue` (`Group` where `Type = 'Queue'` and `DeveloperName` matches); and the matched branch assigns both `{!$Record.Region__c}` and `{!$Record.OwnerId}` directly, which the triggering save then persists. A fallback branch -- an Account with no region populated -- leaves ownership with the creating user and fires an email alert to Devon rather than silently losing the claim.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the inputs exist before building the logic

Before opening Flow Builder, Devon checks the two things the Flow depends on:

```
Renée Castellano confirms: every Account in Cascade Ridge's org has
a populated custom field, Account.Region__c (West / East), maintained
by Sales Ops whenever an account is created or reassigned.

Devon confirms: West_Service_Queue and East_Service_Queue already
exist as Queues (Setup → Queues), each with Warranty Claim as a
supported object, and the right reps already assigned as queue
members.
```

Both prerequisites check out, so the Flow has something real to read from and somewhere real to deliver to.

## Step 2 -- Start the record-triggered Flow

```
Setup → Quick Find → "Flows" → New Flow → Record-Triggered Flow
  Object:                Warranty Claim
  Trigger:               A record is created
  Entry Conditions:      None -- run on every new claim
  Optimize the Flow for: Actions and Related Records
  When to Run:           Before the record is saved
```

Before-save keeps this fast and avoids a second write to the record -- the Flow only ever needs to touch fields that already live on the Warranty Claim itself.

## Step 3 -- Look up the related Account's region

```
Element: Get Records -- "Get Related Account"
  Object:        Account
  Filter:        Id Equals {!$Record.Account__c}
  Sort Order:    Not required (single match expected)
  How Many:      Only the first record
  Fields:        Region__c
```

## Step 4 -- Branch on the region

```
Element: Decision -- "Determine Service Queue"
  Outcome "Is West":
    {!Get_Related_Account.Region__c} Equals "West"
  Outcome "Is East":
    {!Get_Related_Account.Region__c} Equals "East"
  Default Outcome: "No Region on Account"
```

## Step 5 -- Resolve each queue's Id and set the claim's fields

On the "Is West" path:

```
Element: Get Records -- "Get West Queue"
  Object:    Group
  Filters:   Type Equals "Queue"
             DeveloperName Equals "West_Service_Queue"
  Fields:    Id

Element: Assignment -- "Route to West"
  Set {!$Record.Region__c}  =  "West"
  Set {!$Record.OwnerId}    =  {!Get_West_Queue.Id}
```

On the "Is East" path, the mirror image against `East_Service_Queue`. On the default "No Region on Account" path, Devon leaves `OwnerId` untouched (the claim stays with its creator rather than disappearing) and adds a **Send Email Alert** element notifying him directly, so a data-quality gap on the Account surfaces immediately instead of silently misrouting a customer's claim.

## Step 6 -- Activate and test against real sample claims

```
Flow → Save as "Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing" → Activate
```

The team runs it against real data before calling it done:

```
DEVON:   I'm creating three test claims -- one against a known West
         account, one against a known East account, and one against
         an account with no region set, just to prove the fallback
         works.

HANNAH:  The West one just showed up in my team's queue list view --
         Region shows "West," owner is West_Service_Queue. That's
         exactly right.

TOBIAS:  Same on my side for the East claim.

DEVON:   And the no-region test sent me an alert instead of routing
         anywhere silently, like it should.
```

With all three cases behaving exactly as designed, Devon ships the Flow and moves on to building the reporting layer Service leadership needs on top of all this.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing as a before-save, record-triggered Flow on create of Warranty_Claim__c: a Get Records lookup on the related Account's Region__c, a Decision branch, a second Get Records lookup against the Group (Queue) object to resolve West_Service_Queue or East_Service_Queue's Id, and a direct assignment to $Record.Region__c and $Record.OwnerId so the whole thing resolves in a single save. A default branch alerts me by email if an Account has no region set rather than silently misrouting the claim.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: New warranty claims now route themselves to the correct regional team automatically the instant they're created -- no manual reassignment step for anyone. We tested it against real West and East accounts plus an edge case with missing data, and it behaved correctly in every scenario before we turned it on for everyone.
workplaceExplanation.executive: A new warranty claim now reaches the right regional service team immediately and automatically, with no manual handoff step that could introduce delay or error. We tested this against real customer accounts before switching it on.

lessons.title: Building the Reports and Dashboard for Service Leadership
lessons.summary: Devon builds the Warranty Claims by Region report and a Service Leadership dashboard -- claims by status, by region, and aging past SLA -- delivering on the reporting plan from lesson 7, with Marisol Fontaine reviewing the cross-region numbers herself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Claims are flowing in, getting auto-routed, and getting worked -- now Service leadership needs to actually see what's happening across both regions without asking Devon to pull numbers by hand. This lesson builds the reporting layer the team planned out back in lesson 7: a report called **Warranty Claims by Region**, and a supporting dashboard, **Service Leadership Warranty Dashboard**, that together show claim volume by status, by region, and how many open claims have aged past Cascade Ridge's service-level target.

Devon builds a custom report type first, then the report itself, then the dashboard on top of it, and finally walks Marisol Fontaine through the numbers herself -- as VP of Customer Service, she sits above both regions in the org chart, so the totals she sees are the real, complete picture across West and East both.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a scoreboard at a game that's being played on two fields at once, West field and East field. Right now, nobody at Cascade Ridge has a scoreboard at all -- just a pile of individual claim folders. This lesson builds that scoreboard: how many claims are open, how many are closed, how many are stuck waiting too long, broken out by each field and by what stage they're in.

Devon builds the report that counts everything up correctly, then turns it into a dashboard with charts anyone in leadership can glance at. He shows it to Marisol, the VP who oversees both fields at once, and she checks the numbers and confirms they look right. That's where this lesson ends -- the scoreboard works for the person watching the whole game.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Reporting on `Warranty_Claim__c` needs a custom report type before it needs a report, since the standard report-type auto-generated for a new custom object won't necessarily expose the Account relationship the way leadership needs it grouped.

Devon builds **Warranty Claims with Accounts** as a custom report type (primary object: Warranty Claim; secondary: Accounts; category: Customer Support), then builds **Warranty Claims by Region** as a Summary report grouped first by `Region__c`, then by `Status__c`, with `Claim_Amount__c` summed per group, plus a row-level formula computing days-open and a bucket field grouping that into an SLA-aging view (0-3 / 4-7 / 8+ days). A second, narrower report, **Warranty Claims Aging Past SLA**, filters to open claims past the bucket threshold and feeds a dedicated dashboard table. The dashboard itself, **Service Leadership Warranty Dashboard**, is built with its running user set explicitly to a specified user rather than "run as viewer" -- a deliberate, completely standard choice for a leadership dashboard, so every viewer sees the same authoritative numbers regardless of their own access. Marisol Fontaine, as VP of Customer Service, sits genuinely above both the West and East branches in the role hierarchy, so the totals she reviews are correct and complete across both regions -- which is exactly what gets confirmed and signed off in this lesson.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Build the custom report type first

```
Setup → Quick Find → "Report Types" → New Custom Report Type
  Primary Object:    Warranty Claim
  Secondary Object:  Accounts
  Category:          Customer Support
  Label:             Warranty Claims with Accounts
  Deployment:         Deployed
```

This gives the report builder access to both claim-level fields and account-level fields (like the customer's name) in one place, which the standard auto-generated report type wouldn't cleanly expose.

## Step 2 -- Build the primary report

```
Reports → New Report → Report Type: Warranty Claims with Accounts
  Format:        Summary
  Group Rows By: Region__c, then Status__c
  Columns:       Claim Number, Account Name, Product__c,
                 Purchase_Date__c, Claim_Amount__c (Sum), Owner
```

To surface aging, Devon adds a row-level formula column:

```
Row-Level Formula: "Days Open"
  Formula:  TODAY() - DATEVALUE(CreatedDate)
  Format:   Number

Bucket Field: "SLA Status" (built on Days Open)
  0-3 days  → "On Track"
  4-7 days  → "Watch"
  8+ days   → "Past SLA"
```

Saved as **Warranty Claims by Region**, this single report now answers all three questions leadership asked for in lesson 7: volume by region, volume by status, and how many claims have drifted past the service-level target.

## Step 3 -- Build the supporting SLA-focused report

For the dashboard table specifically, Devon builds one narrower report so the "past SLA" view doesn't get buried inside the bigger grouped report:

```
Reports → New Report → Report Type: Warranty Claims with Accounts
  Filters:       Status__c not equal to "Closed"
                 SLA Status equals "Past SLA"
  Columns:       Claim Number, Account Name, Region__c, Status__c,
                 Days Open, Owner
  Sort:          Days Open, descending
```

Saved as **Warranty Claims Aging Past SLA**.

## Step 4 -- Build the dashboard

```
Dashboards → New Dashboard
  Name: Service Leadership Warranty Dashboard

Component 1: Vertical Bar Chart
  Source: Warranty Claims by Region
  Grouping: Region__c, broken out by Status__c

Component 2: Metric
  Source: Warranty Claims by Region
  Value: Count of records, filtered to Status__c not equal "Closed"
  Label: "Total Open Claims"

Component 3: Table
  Source: Warranty Claims Aging Past SLA
  Columns: Claim Number, Account Name, Region__c, Days Open, Owner
```

For the running user, Devon deliberately sets:

```
Dashboard Properties → View dashboard as:
  "A specified user" → Marisol Fontaine
```

so every viewer -- regardless of their own access -- sees the same authoritative, leadership-level numbers, which is standard practice for an executive dashboard.

## Step 5 -- Walk Marisol through it

```
DEVON:    This pulls everything together -- claims by region, by
          status, and anything that's drifted past our service
          target. Take a look and tell me if the shape of this
          matches what you'd expect.

MARISOL:  This is exactly the view I asked for in our planning
          session. I can see both regions side by side, and the
          "past SLA" table is going to be genuinely useful in our
          weekly leadership check-in. The totals line up with what
          I'd estimate just from the volume I've been hearing about.

DEVON:    I'll share the dashboard folder with you, Hannah, and
          Tobias so it's available to the whole leadership group
          going forward.
```

With Marisol's review signed off and the dashboard shared out to the folder, Devon moves on to the next phase of the build -- Service leadership now has a single place to see how the warranty program is actually running.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a custom report type (Warranty Claims with Accounts), the Warranty Claims by Region summary report with a row-level formula and bucket field for SLA aging, a supporting Warranty Claims Aging Past SLA report, and the Service Leadership Warranty Dashboard with its running user explicitly set to Marisol Fontaine so every viewer sees consistent, authoritative numbers. Shared the dashboard folder with Marisol, Hannah, and Tobias.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Service leadership now has a single dashboard showing warranty claim volume by region and status, plus which claims have aged past our service target -- exactly the view we scoped out in planning. Marisol reviewed it and confirmed the numbers match her expectations.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Customer service leadership can now see, at a glance, how warranty claims are moving across both regions and which ones need attention before they age too long. This closes a visibility gap leadership didn't have before.

lessons.title: Testing With Real Users Before Rollout
lessons.summary: Before rollout, Devon runs a hands-on UAT pass with real reps and both regional managers -- creating sample claims, checking the Flow routes them correctly, and confirming the day-to-day workflow holds up.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Warranty_Claim__c built, secured, automated, and reported on, this lesson is the last checkpoint before Cascade Ridge Outfitters' roughly 150 users ever touch it: user acceptance testing. Devon Okafor pulls together a small, real test group -- a handful of West and East Service Reps plus both regional managers, Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren -- and walks them through creating genuine sample Warranty_Claim__c records the way a rep actually would on a real support call: picking a Product__c, logging a Purchase_Date__c and Issue_Description__c, setting Region__c, and saving.

The UAT pass checks the things that break a rollout on day one if nobody catches them first: does the Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing Flow actually drop a new West claim into West_Service_Queue and an East claim into East_Service_Queue every time, do the page layout and required fields make sense to someone who's never seen the object before, does Claim_Amount__c format and validate the way Finance expects, and can a rep edit Status__c and Resolution_Notes__c on their own record without hitting a sharing wall. Devon also gives Hannah and Tobias a guided look at the finished "Warranty Claims by Region" report and dashboard so they know it exists and know where to find it. What this pass does not include is either regional manager logging in under their own credentials and checking that report filtered to just their own team's numbers -- there's no reason yet to think that would show anything different from what Devon or Marisol sees, so nobody specifically tests it that way.
lessons.explainSimple: Before a new store opens to the public, the owner usually asks a few real employees to run through a normal day first -- ring up a sale, restock a shelf, handle a return -- to catch anything confusing or broken while it's still just a dry run. That's what this lesson is. Devon asks a few real reps and both regional managers to use the new warranty claim form the way they actually would on a busy day: filing a claim, watching it land in the right bin for someone to pick up, and making notes about it. Everyone walks through it, nods that it works, and gets ready for the real doors to open. Nobody happens to check every single drawer from every single person's own key, though -- they check that the drawers exist and that stuff gets filed into them correctly, which feels like enough for now.
lessons.explainProfessional:
UAT exists to catch exactly the class of problem that unit-level configuration checks can't: whether the thing you built actually fits how real people work, under real conditions, before 150 of them hit it at once. Devon's test plan is appropriately scoped to that goal -- functional correctness of the object, the Flow, and the layout, exercised by the actual population who will use it daily. Recruiting real West and East reps plus both regional managers, rather than testing solo as the admin, is the right instinct, because an admin's own access (effectively a System Administrator profile, which bypasses sharing rules entirely) tells you nothing about what a Service Rep or a Service Manager will actually see.

The gap, invisible at the time, is a scoping choice rather than an oversight anyone would flag: the UAT script verifies that reps can create and own their records cleanly, and that the Flow and reports exist and look right from an admin's-eye view. It never asks either regional manager to authenticate as themselves and pull the "Warranty Claims by Region" report filtered to only their own team's open claims. Visibility into a manager's own team's records is a role-hierarchy-and-sharing-rule question, not a page-layout-and-Flow question, and nothing in a reasonably thorough functional UAT naturally forces that specific check unless someone writes it into the script on purpose. That's the exact blind spot this UAT, done well by every other measure, still carries into go-live.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Recruit a UAT group that matches the real org, not just the admin's view

Devon pulls together six participants instead of testing alone: three West Service Reps, two East Service Reps, and both regional managers, Hannah Reyes (West) and Tobias Lindgren (East). Testing only under his own Salesforce Administrator profile would prove nothing about what a Service Rep or Service Manager profile can actually do -- Devon's own access bypasses every sharing rule on the org.

## Step 2 -- Script the test around a real support call, not an abstract checklist

Each rep gets the same scenario to run through, once for a West product and once for an East product where applicable:

```
UAT SCRIPT -- Warranty_Claim__c, Scenario 1

1. Open the Account for a real test customer.
2. New Warranty Claim.
3. Product__c: "TrailBlazer 45L Pack"
4. Purchase_Date__c: a date within the last 12 months
5. Issue_Description__c: "Zipper pull separated from main
   compartment after 3 months of normal use."
6. Region__c: West
7. Save.
8. Confirm the claim appears with Status__c defaulted to "New."
```

## Step 3 -- Confirm the Flow routes every claim correctly, every time

Immediately after each rep saves a claim, Devon checks that Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing fired and the record landed in the right queue:

```
Warranty Claim: WC-00142
Region__c: West
Expected Queue: West_Service_Queue
Owner (after Flow runs): West_Service_Queue  -- confirmed
```

He repeats this for every West and East claim created during the session, and deliberately creates one claim with Region__c left blank to confirm the Flow's fault path doesn't silently misroute it -- it leaves the claim unassigned for manual triage instead.

## Step 4 -- Watch reps use the layout cold, without coaching them through it

Devon doesn't walk reps through the screen -- he hands them the scenario card and watches where they hesitate. Two real findings come out of this session: the Issue_Description__c field isn't marked required on the page layout even though it should be (reps sometimes skip it), and Claim_Amount__c needs a currency hint added because two reps weren't sure whether to type "150" or "$150.00." Both go into a short issues list and get fixed before go-live.

## Step 5 -- Have reps edit their own records, the way they will during a real claim's life

Each rep reopens their own claim, updates Status__c to "In Review," and adds a note to Resolution_Notes__c -- confirming record ownership and edit behavior both work smoothly for the person who actually owns the record. No sharing issue shows up here, because Private OWD plus "can edit your own record" is the simplest case there is -- it's the only case this UAT ever actually puts under test.

## Step 6 -- Walk both regional managers through the reporting layer -- as Devon drives it

With reps done, Devon brings Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren into a short session and pulls up the "Warranty Claims by Region" report and dashboard himself, filtering it live to show West numbers, then East numbers. Both managers watch the numbers track the test claims just created and say it looks right. Neither logs into their own account to pull the same report filtered to just their own region from their own screen -- Devon's screen share stands in for that check, and nothing in the test plan calls for anything more.

## Step 7 -- Log issues, fix the quick ones, and get sign-off

```
UAT ISSUE LOG -- Warranty_Claim__c
1. Issue_Description__c not marked required on page layout. FIXED.
2. Claim_Amount__c needs a currency format hint in help text. FIXED.
3. Blank Region__c claim correctly skipped by Auto_Routing Flow,
   left unassigned for manual triage. Confirmed working as intended.
```

Devon shares the issue log and a short demo recording with Marisol Fontaine, who signs off that the team is ready to roll out to the full ~150 users. The reps' experience is clean, the Flow is reliable, and the reporting layer looks correct from every screen it's been checked on so far.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran UAT with 3 West reps, 2 East reps, and both regional managers against real Warranty_Claim__c scenarios. Confirmed Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing correctly routes West/East claims to West_Service_Queue/East_Service_Queue and leaves blank-Region claims unassigned for manual triage. Fixed two issues (Issue_Description__c not required, Claim_Amount__c needs a currency hint). Demoed Warranty Claims by Region report to Hannah and Tobias from my own screen; didn't have either of them pull it from their own login.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: UAT is complete with real reps and both regional managers participating, not just Devon testing solo. Two minor issues were found and fixed before go-live. Everyone involved -- reps and managers alike -- confirmed the process works and the numbers look right, and Marisol has signed off to proceed to full rollout.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before rolling this out to the whole Sales and Service organization, we tested it with real reps and both regional managers handling real-looking claims. It held up well, a couple of small fixes were made, and the team that will use it every day has confirmed it's ready.

lessons.title: Rolling Out to Sales and Service Teams
lessons.summary: Warranty_Claim__c goes live for all ~150 Cascade Ridge Outfitters users -- training sessions for reps and managers, a rollout announcement from Marisol Fontaine, and a smooth go-live.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
UAT is signed off. This lesson is the actual rollout: taking Warranty_Claim__c, the Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing Flow, the security model, and the "Warranty Claims by Region" report live for all roughly 150 Cascade Ridge Outfitters users across Sales and Service. Devon Okafor runs three short live training sessions -- one for West Service Reps, one for East Service Reps, and a combined session for both regional managers plus Renée Castellano, Sales Operations Lead, since Sales needs to understand how a warranty claim links back to the Account and Contact records they already work with daily.

Marisol Fontaine, as the business sponsor, sends the official rollout announcement -- a short email and a pinned Chatter post -- setting the go-live date and pointing everyone to Devon's one-page quick reference guide. On go-live day, Devon watches the first real claims come in from across both regions, confirms the Flow is routing them cleanly, and checks in with a few reps directly. By end of day, the team is calling it a clean launch: real claims are flowing in from day one, nobody's stuck, and the rollout feels like exactly the kind of quiet, uneventful go-live everyone hopes for.
lessons.explainSimple: Picture a new ride opening at an amusement park. Before the gates open to everyone, the park already tested it with a few staff members (that was the last lesson). Now it's opening weekend for real: there's a sign explaining how the ride works, a short walkthrough for the staff running it, and the park's manager tells everyone over the intercom that it's open. On opening day, people start riding it, nothing breaks, and everyone goes home happy. That's this lesson -- the warranty claim process opens for real, to everyone, with a little training and an announcement from the person in charge, and the first day goes smoothly.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A UAT sign-off answers "does this work." Rollout answers a different question: "can 150 people who weren't in the test room pick this up smoothly on day one." That gap is why training and a clear announcement matter even after a clean UAT pass -- the handful of reps who tested it already have a mental model of the object; the other roughly 140 users don't.

Splitting training by audience is deliberate: West and East Service Reps need the hands-on claim-creation workflow drilled in session, while the combined manager-and-Sales-Ops session is lighter on data entry and heavier on context -- where a warranty claim fits relative to the Account and Contact records Renée Castellano's Sales team already touches, and what the regional managers should expect to see once claims start flowing. Having Marisol Fontaine, not Devon, send the rollout announcement matters organizationally too: a system change arriving from the business sponsor reads as a business priority, not an IT project being pushed onto people's plates. The go-live itself is uneventful by design -- that's what a well-sequenced rollout, sitting on top of a UAT pass that already caught the layout and Flow issues, is supposed to look like. Nothing here yet tests whether every piece of the security model behind the scenes was actually built correctly; it tests whether the system people can see and touch works. That distinction matters a few weeks from now.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Split training by what each audience actually needs

Devon schedules three 30-minute sessions instead of one all-hands session, because West/East reps, managers, and Sales Ops need different depth:

```
TRAINING SCHEDULE -- Warranty_Claim__c Rollout
  Session 1: West Service Reps (approx. 55 users)
  Session 2: East Service Reps (approx. 50 users)
  Session 3: Regional Managers + Sales Ops
             (Hannah Reyes, Tobias Lindgren, Renée Castellano
              + ~40 Sales users)
```

## Step 2 -- Build a one-page quick reference guide

Rather than relying on memory from a single training session, Devon writes a one-pager covering the fields every rep fills in, what happens automatically (the Flow routing to West_Service_Queue or East_Service_Queue), and who to contact with questions:

```
QUICK REFERENCE -- Filing a Warranty Claim
1. Open the customer's Account.
2. New Warranty Claim > fill Product__c, Purchase_Date__c,
   Issue_Description__c, Region__c.
3. Save -- it routes itself to the right regional queue automatically.
4. Track progress on Status__c. Questions: Devon Okafor.
```

## Step 3 -- Confirm permission sets and profile access before anyone logs a real claim

Devon double-checks that every West and East Service Rep's profile has Create/Read/Edit on Warranty_Claim__c, that both regional managers and Renée Castellano have at least Read access on the object and its fields, and that the West_Service_Queue and East_Service_Queue each have the right queue members assigned so claims routed by the Flow actually show up for someone to work:

```
Setup > Queues > West_Service_Queue
  Queue Members: Hannah Reyes, West Service Rep 1, West Service Rep 2,
                 West Service Rep 3

Setup > Queues > East_Service_Queue
  Queue Members: Tobias Lindgren, East Service Rep 1, East Service Rep 2
```

## Step 4 -- Run the Service Rep training sessions hands-on

Each rep session is live, not a slide deck -- reps create one real sample claim during the call, following the same scenario style used in UAT, so their first real experience with the object happens with Devon watching, not alone on a live customer call. Devon also shows reps how to find a claim that's landed in their region's queue and assign it to themselves to start working it.

## Step 5 -- Run the manager and Sales Ops session with different content

Hannah Reyes, Tobias Lindgren, and Renée Castellano get a session focused on context rather than data entry: how a Warranty_Claim__c relates to the Account and Contact records Sales already owns, where the "Warranty Claims by Region" report lives, and what each manager should expect once real claims start flowing from their team. Devon demos the dashboard again in this session -- from his own screen, as in UAT -- confirming the numbers look right before anyone's relying on them for real.

## Step 6 -- Marisol sends the rollout announcement

```
From: Marisol Fontaine, VP of Customer Service
Subject: Warranty Claims Go Live Monday

Starting Monday, all warranty claims for Cascade Ridge Outfitters
products should be filed in Salesforce using the new Warranty Claim
record. Training recordings and the quick reference guide are linked
below. This replaces our old email/spreadsheet process effective

lessons.title: Regional Managers Can't See Their Own Team's Claims
lessons.summary: A few weeks after go-live, Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren each report their region's report shows almost no open claims -- and Devon traces it to the Role Hierarchy itself, not the sharing rule.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A few weeks into go-live, the smooth launch from the last lesson runs into its first real problem. Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren each separately bring the same complaint to Devon Okafor: their "Warranty Claims by Region" report shows almost no open claims for their own team, even though they know for a fact their reps are actively filing real claims every day. Both managers initially assume it's a report filter mistake -- a date range set wrong, or a field filter excluding active statuses.

This lesson is Devon's investigation. He checks the obvious, correctly-built pieces first: the Organization-Wide Default for Warranty_Claim__c is Private, exactly as designed, and the Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility sharing rule -- the role-hierarchy-based rule meant to give managers visibility into their team's claims -- looks correctly configured when he opens it in Setup. Neither of those is the problem. The actual cause only turns up when Devon opens Setup > Roles and looks at the real Role Hierarchy tree: Hannah and Tobias are sitting at the exact same level as their own Service Reps, both assigned directly under "VP of Customer Service" as peers of the reps, not above them. Role-hierarchy-based sharing only ever extends access upward to roles genuinely above a record owner's role in the tree -- and because Hannah and Tobias were never placed above their own reps, the sharing rule has nothing to extend to them, no matter how correctly it was built. The lesson ends at that discovery -- understood, not yet fixed.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a company org chart where, by mistake, a store manager got drawn on the chart standing right next to the cashiers instead of above them. The rule at this company is: a manager automatically gets to see everything the people below them on the chart are doing. If the manager isn't actually drawn above anyone, that rule has nobody to apply to -- the manager just looks like one more cashier on the page, even though everyone still calls them "manager" and expects them to see the whole team's work.

That's exactly what Devon finds. Hannah and Tobias are supposed to see everything their own reps are doing, the same way a manager sees their team's work. But when Devon looks at the actual org chart inside Salesforce, Hannah and Tobias aren't drawn above their reps at all -- they're drawn right next to them, at the same level. The rule that was supposed to give them visibility had nothing to reach down into, because there was no "down" from where they were sitting.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The diagnostic discipline here matters as much as the finding itself: Devon works outward from the parts of the security model most likely to be wrong by habit (OWD, sharing rule) before looking at the part that's easy to assume is fine simply because "the hierarchy already exists." Private OWD on Warranty_Claim__c checks out -- that was the deliberate design decision from earlier in this build. Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility, when opened in Setup, is also configured exactly as a role-hierarchy sharing rule should be: it grants Read/Write access based on role, extending from a record owner's role upward.

The actual defect isn't in either of those -- it's structural, in the Role Hierarchy tree itself. Role-hierarchy-based sharing in Salesforce works by a simple mechanical rule: a user automatically inherits visibility into records owned by any user whose role sits below their own role in the hierarchy tree, full stop, regardless of how correctly any sharing rule layered on top of that hierarchy is built. If Hannah Reyes's role and her West Service Reps' roles sit at the same level -- both direct children of "VP of Customer Service," siblings rather than parent-and-child -- then there is no "below" relationship for the hierarchy engine to act on. The sharing rule Devon built correctly has a real mechanism to extend; it simply has nothing underneath Hannah or Tobias to extend it to. This is the kind of defect that survives a correct implementation of every component built around it, because none of those components are actually broken -- the tree they all depend on is shaped wrong one level too high.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Two managers, the same complaint, independently

Hannah Reyes messages Devon first: "My Warranty Claims by Region report is showing almost nothing for West -- maybe four open claims. My reps have filed way more than that this month." Two days later, Tobias Lindgren raises the same issue for East, unprompted, in a separate conversation. Devon treats the fact that it hit both regions, independently, as the first real clue -- a one-off report filter mistake wouldn't hit two different people's reports the same way at the same time.

## Step 2 -- Rule out the obvious suspect: the report itself

```
Report: Warranty Claims by Region
Filter: Status__c != "Closed"
Group by: Region__c
Run As: Hannah Reyes (via "Run Report As" preview)
Result: 4 rows returned for West
```

Devon confirms the report's own filters and grouping are correct -- no date range mistake, no wrong field. Run as Hannah, it genuinely only returns four records, even though a quick ownership count confirms far more West claims exist in the org overall.

## Step 3 -- Check the Organization-Wide Default

```
Setup > Security > Sharing Settings > Warranty_Claim__c
Default Internal Access: Private
```

Correct, and exactly as designed -- no changes needed here.

## Step 4 -- Check the sharing rule that's supposed to cover this

```
Setup > Sharing Settings > Warranty_Claim__c Sharing Rules
Rule: Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility
Based on: Role Hierarchy (owner's role, and roles below)
Grants: Read/Write
```

The rule is configured the way a role-hierarchy sharing rule should be. Nothing about its setup explains four records instead of dozens.

## Step 5 -- Open the actual Role Hierarchy tree

This is the step that finally surfaces it:

```
Setup > Users > Roles > Role Hierarchy (tree view)

VP of Customer Service
  |-- Hannah Reyes (West Region Service Manager)
  |-- Tobias Lindgren (East Region Service Manager)
  |-- [West Service Rep 1]
  |-- [West Service Rep 2]
  |-- [West Service Rep 3]
  |-- [East Service Rep 1]
  +-- [East Service Rep 2]
```

Hannah and Tobias sit directly under "VP of Customer Service," at the exact same level as every Service Rep -- peers, not parents. No "Regional Service Manager -- West" or "-- East" role was ever created to sit between the VP role and the reps.

## Step 6 -- Confirm the mechanism, not just the symptom

Devon reasons it through in his notes: role-hierarchy sharing only ever extends visibility to roles sitting above a record's owner in this tree. Since Hannah and Tobias aren't above their own reps -- they're beside them -- the correctly-built Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility rule has no "below" to extend into for either of them. It works perfectly for Marisol Fontaine, whose VP role genuinely does sit above everyone, which is exactly why nobody caught this until a manager one level down went looking.

## Step 7 -- Write up the diagnosis before touching anything

```
DIAGNOSIS -- Warranty Claims by Region underreporting
Root cause: Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren are assigned directly
under "VP of Customer Service," as peers of their own Service Reps,
not above them in the Role Hierarchy. No regional manager role was
ever created between the VP role and the reps.
OWD: Private -- correct, unchanged.
Sharing rule Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility: correctly configured,
unchanged. It has nothing to extend to for Hannah or Tobias because
neither sits above their reps in the hierarchy.
Status: Diagnosed. Not yet fixed.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Confirmed OWD (Private) and the Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility sharing rule are both correctly configured -- neither is the cause. Opened Setup > Roles and found Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren sitting directly under VP of Customer Service as peers of their own Service Reps, not above them. Role-hierarchy sharing has nothing to extend into from either manager's position. Diagnosed, not yet fixed.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Both regional managers reported the same visibility problem independently. We've traced the root cause to how the Role Hierarchy itself was structured when it was originally set up -- not to anything wrong with the security rule we built on top of it. We know exactly what's wrong and are moving to fix it next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found why our regional service managers weren't seeing their teams' full claim volume in reporting -- it comes down to how reporting lines were originally set up in the system, not a flaw in the security design itself. We now understand the issue precisely and are correcting it immediately.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing the Role Hierarchy Gap
lessons.summary: Devon adds two regional manager roles above the reps, reassigns everyone into the corrected hierarchy, confirms the existing sharing rule needs no changes, and sets a standing review process so this can't slip through again.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 found exactly what's wrong: Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren were assigned as peers of their own Service Reps in the Role Hierarchy, not above them, so the correctly-built Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility sharing rule had nothing to extend visibility into. This lesson is the fix, in five concrete parts. First, Devon creates two new roles directly under "VP of Customer Service": "Regional Service Manager -- West" and "Regional Service Manager -- East." Second, he reassigns Hannah Reyes to the West role and Tobias Lindgren to the East role. Third, he reassigns every West Service Rep to report under "Regional Service Manager -- West," and every East Service Rep under "Regional Service Manager -- East," instead of directly under the VP role.

Fourth, Devon confirms that the existing Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility sharing rule now works correctly with zero changes to the rule itself -- Hannah and Tobias can finally see their own region's claims in the "Warranty Claims by Region" report, and Marisol Fontaine, sitting above the whole corrected tree, still sees everything. Fifth, and just as important as the technical fix, Devon writes up a standing process: any time a new role or team structure gets added to Salesforce going forward, the team reviews the Role Hierarchy diagram against the real org chart before go-live, specifically asking whether every manager who needs record visibility is actually positioned above their team in the tree -- not just confirming that every rep can create and own their own records cleanly.
lessons.explainSimple:
Back to the org chart that had the manager drawn next to the cashiers instead of above them: the fix is exactly what it sounds like -- redraw the chart correctly. Add a clear manager box above the cashiers, move the manager into it, and move the cashiers underneath that box instead of directly under the store owner. Once the chart is actually shaped the right way, the same old rule -- "managers automatically see what's below them" -- works perfectly, with nothing about the rule itself needing to change. The chart was the problem the whole time, not the rule.

And going forward, before anyone adds a new box to that chart, someone double-checks it against how the real team actually works -- not just "can everyone do their own job," but "can every manager actually see their own team's work from where they're standing on the chart."
lessons.explainProfessional:
The fix is deliberately structural, not a workaround layered on top of the existing problem. Rather than writing a second, manager-specific sharing rule to patch around Hannah's and Tobias's missing position in the hierarchy -- which would have worked, narrowly, but left the underlying Role Hierarchy permanently wrong and created a second rule to maintain forever -- Devon corrects the actual shape of the tree. Two new roles, "Regional Service Manager -- West" and "Regional Service Manager -- East," are inserted as direct children of "VP of Customer Service." Hannah and Tobias move into those roles, and every Service Rep in each region gets reparented under the matching new role instead of sitting directly under the VP.

Confirming step four -- that Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility needs no changes at all -- is the detail that proves the diagnosis from Lesson 15 was correct, not just plausible. If the rule itself had needed modification to work, the root cause wouldn't have been purely structural. Because the rule was already built correctly against role-hierarchy semantics, correcting the hierarchy underneath it is sufficient on its own; Hannah and Tobias now sit genuinely above their own reps, so the rule's existing "owner's role and roles below" logic reaches them automatically, and Marisol's position at the top of the entire tree is undisturbed.

The process change matters at least as much as the technical fix, because it's the only thing that prevents a structurally identical bug from recurring the next time a team or role gets added. The standing review asks a sharper, more specific question than "does the org chart look complete" -- it asks, for every manager being added, whether that manager's role is positioned above the team they need to see, as distinct from whether every individual contributor can create and own their own records. Those are two genuinely different questions, and this entire incident exists because the build only ever checked the second one.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Create the two missing roles

```
Setup > Users > Roles > Role Hierarchy
  Click "Add Role" under "VP of Customer Service"

  Role Name: Regional Service Manager -- West
  Role Name: Regional Service Manager -- East

New tree (partial):
VP of Customer Service
  |-- Regional Service Manager -- West
  |-- Regional Service Manager -- East
  |-- Hannah Reyes (West Region Service Manager)  [not moved yet]
  |-- Tobias Lindgren (East Region Service Manager) [not moved yet]
  |-- [West Service Reps...]
  +-- [East Service Reps...]
```

## Step 2 -- Reassign Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren into the new roles

```
Setup > Users > Hannah Reyes > Edit
  Role: Regional Service Manager -- West

Setup > Users > Tobias Lindgren > Edit
  Role: Regional Service Manager -- East
```

Devon uses Salesforce's role reassignment flow rather than editing records piecemeal where possible, so record ownership and existing sharing recalculate cleanly as each move happens.

## Step 3 -- Reassign every West and East Service Rep under the new regional roles

```
For each West Service Rep user record:
  Role: West Service Rep  ->  reparent under Regional Service Manager -- West

For each East Service Rep user record:
  Role: East Service Rep  ->  reparent under Regional Service Manager -- East

Corrected tree:
VP of Customer Service
  |-- Regional Service Manager -- West (Hannah Reyes)
  |     |-- West Service Rep 1
  |     |-- West Service Rep 2
  |     +-- West Service Rep 3
  +-- Regional Service Manager -- East (Tobias Lindgren)
        |-- East Service Rep 1
        +-- East Service Rep 2
```

Devon runs this as a controlled, off-peak change and lets Salesforce's automatic sharing recalculation complete fully (a background job, visible in Setup > Jobs > Sharing Recalculation) before validating anything.

## Step 4 -- Confirm the existing sharing rule needs no changes at all

```
Setup > Sharing Settings > Warranty_Claim__c Sharing Rules
Rule: Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility
Based on: Role Hierarchy (owner's role and roles below)
Grants: Read/Write
-- No edits made to this rule. --

Run Report As: Hannah Reyes
Report: Warranty Claims by Region (filtered to West)
Result: full, correct count of open West claims
```

Devon repeats the "Run Report As" check for Tobias Lindgren against East, and separately confirms Marisol Fontaine's view is unchanged -- she still sees every claim across both regions, since her VP role still sits above the entire corrected tree.

## Step 5 -- Write the standing process so this can't recur

```
STANDING PROCESS -- Role Hierarchy Review (effective immediately)

Before any new role or team structure goes live in Salesforce,
Devon's team reviews the Role Hierarchy diagram against the real
org chart and checks, for every manager being added:

  1. Can every rep on this team create and own their own records?
     (the question the original build already checked)
  2. Is every manager who needs record visibility actually
     positioned ABOVE their team in this tree -- not beside it?
     (the question that was missed, and the one that matters just
     as much)

Both questions get signed off before go-live, not just the first one.
```

## Step 6 -- Close the loop with Hannah, Tobias, and Marisol

Devon confirms with Hannah and Tobias directly that their region's numbers in "Warranty Claims by Region" now match what they know is actually happening on their teams, and shares the standing process document with Marisol as part of closing out the incident. A role hierarchy has to mirror who actually needs to see whose records, not just who needs to create their own -- "can reps own their records" and "can managers see their team's records" turned out to be two different questions, and this build had only ever checked the first one.

Confirmed via Run Report As that Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility needed zero changes -- both managers now see their own region's full claim volume, Marisol's view is unaffected. Added a standing Role Hierarchy review step to the go-live checklist.

Both regional managers have confirmed their numbers now match reality, and we've added a permanent check to our rollout process so this specific mistake can't happen again on a future project.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've corrected the reporting-line structure that was causing our regional managers to miss visibility into their own teams' work, and confirmed both managers now see accurate numbers with no disruption to anyone else's access. We've also put a standing check in place so any future team changes get verified the same way before they go live.

lessons.title: Presenting the Real Results: Visibility Gap Included
lessons.summary: Devon Okafor presents the finished Warranty_Claim__c rollout to Marisol Fontaine and Service leadership -- real adoption numbers, and a plain, unembarrassed account of the role-hierarchy visibility gap that was found and fixed weeks after go-live.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the moment the warranty-claims project has been building toward: Devon Okafor stands in front of Marisol Fontaine, VP of Customer Service, along with Hannah Reyes, Tobias Lindgren, and Renee Castellano, and presents the system as it actually stands today -- not the system as it was designed on a whiteboard months ago. `Warranty_Claim__c` is live, OWD is Private, the `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` sharing rule is in production, the `Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing` flow is routing every new claim to the right region automatically, and roughly 150 users across Sales and Service are using it instead of tracking warranty issues by email and memory. That's the real win, and it gets stated plainly, first.

But this presentation also has to cover the part that didn't go smoothly: a few weeks after go-live, Hannah and Tobias each separately told Devon that the Warranty Claims by Region dashboard was showing almost none of their own team's claims. Devon has to explain, in front of the VP who sponsored this project, exactly what that was, why the carefully-built sharing rule didn't catch it, how it was found, and how it was fixed. The skill in this video is choosing to lead with that story instead of hoping nobody asks about it -- and framing it as evidence the team's own review process works, not as a confession to get through quickly.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a store puts in a brand-new cash register system so every clerk's sales get tracked automatically instead of written on a paper pad. The system works great -- except for one wrinkle: when they first set it up, the store manager's own name got typed into the org chart as just another clerk instead of as the person above the clerks, so for a few weeks the manager's own sales reports showed almost nothing from their own team, even though the clerks were ringing up sales just fine.

That's exactly what happened at Cascade Ridge Outfitters. The new warranty-claim system worked -- claims were being logged, routed, and resolved instead of lost in email. But the chart that says who manages whom had Hannah and Tobias listed as if they were just two more reps standing next to their teams, instead of above them. So their own dashboards showed almost nothing. Devon found it, fixed the chart, and now tells the VP exactly what happened and why it's fixed for good -- instead of just saying "everything's great" and hoping nobody notices.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A leadership presentation about a Salesforce rollout succeeds or fails on the same decision every honest retrospective turns on: whether the presenter treats the working system as the deliverable, or treats an uninterrupted success narrative as the deliverable. Devon's presentation here does the former. The headline is real: `Warranty_Claim__c` with OWD Private, a correctly-built sharing rule, Flow-driven auto-routing, and live reporting, in daily use by roughly 150 users. That's worth stating plainly and first, because it's true and it's the thing Marisol actually sponsored.

Naming the visibility gap specifically -- rather than alluding to "some early adoption friction" -- matters for the same reason a named root cause always matters more than a vague one: it's what lets the room trust the fix, not just the apology. The mechanism is mechanical and explainable without jargon: Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren were placed directly under "VP of Customer Service" in the Role Hierarchy as peers of their own Service Reps, rather than as parent roles above them. `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` was built correctly -- it extends visibility up the Role Hierarchy exactly the way a sharing rule is supposed to -- but a correctly-built sharing rule has nothing to extend when the hierarchy itself doesn't reflect who actually manages whom. Record ownership (who owns a given `Warranty_Claim__c`) and hierarchy-based visibility (who can see records owned by people below them) are two different questions, and this gap is what happens when the second one is assumed to follow automatically from getting the first one right.

The reframe that makes this presentation land is simple and honest: catching this through Hannah and Tobias noticing their own numbers looked wrong, rather than through months of silent bad decisions downstream, is the process working -- and the fix (new "Regional Service Manager" roles placed correctly above their reps) required zero changes to the sharing rule itself, which is exactly what you'd expect if the rule was sound all along and the hierarchy underneath it was the actual defect.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Open with what's actually being presented, before the gap

Remind the room of the real goal: warranty claims that used to live entirely in reps' email inboxes and phone notes now live in one tracked object, with automatic routing to the right region and a manager's own dashboard showing their team's real numbers. That's the deliverable Marisol sponsored. Everything else in this meeting is about how much that system can actually be trusted.

## Step 2 -- State the real adoption numbers plainly, first

```
WARRANTY CLAIM SYSTEM -- WHAT'S ACTUALLY RUNNING TODAY

Object:        Warranty_Claim__c, live, OWD Private
Users:         ~150 across Sales and Service
Automation:    Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing (Record-Triggered Flow) --
               every new claim auto-routes to the right region
Security:      Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep / _Service_Manager
               permission sets, in use since go-live
Reporting:     "Warranty Claims by Region" report and dashboard,
               refreshed daily
```

Lead with this. A presentation that buries the real, working system under a wall of caveats about the incident reads as more nervous than it needs to be.

## Step 3 -- Name the visibility gap by its exact mechanism

```
DEVON: A few weeks after go-live, Hannah and Tobias each told me
       their own "Warranty Claims by Region" dashboard was showing
       almost none of their team's claims -- even though their reps
       were logging claims correctly every day. The sharing rule we
       built, Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility, was never the
       problem. The Role Hierarchy underneath it was: when we first
       set it up, Hannah and Tobias were placed directly under "VP
       of Customer Service" as peers of their own Service Reps, not
       as roles above them. A sharing rule that extends visibility
       up the hierarchy has nothing to extend when the hierarchy
       doesn't actually show who manages whom.
```

## Step 4 -- Explain why two independent reports were the tell, not the discovery

Say this plainly: "Hannah and Tobias reporting the same kind of problem independently, within the same few weeks, was the signal that this was structural, not a one-off glitch on one person's screen. I checked the actual Role Hierarchy tree in Setup, not the sharing rule first, because two different managers seeing the same gap pointed at something shared underneath both of them."

## Step 5 -- State the fix and why it needed zero changes to the sharing rule

```
FIX: created two new roles, "Regional Service Manager -- West" and
     "Regional Service Manager -- East", directly under VP of
     Customer Service. Reassigned Hannah and Tobias into those roles.
     Reassigned every Service Rep to report under their correct
     regional manager role instead of directly under the VP.
RESULT: Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility needed no changes at all --
     it was already built correctly. Both managers' dashboards now
     show their own team's claims in full.
```

## Step 6 -- Frame the good news correctly

The right frame isn't "we made a mistake and fixed it," it's "our managers noticing their own numbers looked wrong, and us checking the actual org structure instead of guessing, caught this before it ever caused a real staffing or performance decision." No claim was ever lost -- every claim existed and was owned correctly the whole time; only the managers' view of their own team was wrong.

## Step 7 -- Rehearse the hard question

```
Q: How do we know the Role Hierarchy is right everywhere else?
A: We don't know that with certainty for structures we haven't
   touched yet. What changed is that any new role or team structure
   now gets checked against the real org chart before go-live --
   specifically checking manager-to-team visibility, not just rep
   record ownership, which is the exact distinction that caused this.
```

## Step 8 -- Close by asking for explicit sign-off

Ask Marisol, Hannah, and Tobias directly to confirm the dashboards now reflect their real team numbers, and that they understand the standing Role-Hierarchy review step well enough to expect it the next time a team structure changes.

lessons.title: From Claims to Action: How Service Teams Use This Day to Day
lessons.summary: Translating Warranty_Claim__c into Hannah's, Tobias's, and the reps' actual daily workflow -- a claim's real lifecycle from submission to close, who can see and do what, and the honest boundary of what V1 doesn't automate yet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the rollout presented and the visibility gap behind them, this video follows a warranty claim the rest of the way -- out of Setup and into an actual Tuesday on Hannah Reyes's and Tobias Lindgren's Service teams. A customer calls or emails about a defective product; a Service Rep creates the `Warranty_Claim__c` record with `Product__c`, `Purchase_Date__c`, `Issue_Description__c`, and `Region__c`; the `Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing` flow fires on creation and routes it to the right regional queue based on `Region__c`; a rep reviews it, works it, and either approves it (filling in `Resolution_Notes__c` and `Claim_Amount__c`) or denies it with a documented reason, moving `Status__c` to Closed. The `Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep` permission set governs what a rep can see and edit on their own team's claims; `Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager` extends that to a manager's whole region, the same visibility the Lesson 17 fix finally made work correctly for Hannah and Tobias.

This video also states, honestly and without apology, the two things a rep or a customer still cannot do: a customer cannot log in anywhere to check their own claim's status, because there is no customer-facing self-service portal in V1 -- they still call or email a rep, who creates the record on their behalf. And nothing automatically escalates a claim that's sitting open past its SLA window; a manager has to actually look at the "aging past SLA" view on the dashboard to catch that. Both are named here as real, deferred V2 ideas, consistent with what was scoped out back when this object was first designed.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a hiking boot breaks and you call the store that sold it to you. The person on the phone writes down what's wrong, and within a minute a note with your information automatically lands on the desk of whichever regional repair team actually handles your area -- nobody has to manually figure out where to send it. That repair team looks at the note, decides whether it's covered, and either fixes it or explains why not.

That's exactly what happens at Cascade Ridge Outfitters now. A customer calls about a broken product, a rep types up what's wrong, and the system automatically sends it to the right region's team the instant it's saved -- no one has to remember to forward it. The rep working it can see everything they need for their own claims, and their manager can see everything for the whole region. What the system can't do yet: the customer themselves can't go check on their own claim online, they still have to call back and ask. And if a claim just sits there too long without anyone touching it, nothing automatically rings an alarm -- a manager has to actually go look at the list of overdue claims to notice.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The value of a well-designed object is only realized the moment it maps cleanly onto a real daily workflow -- a technically correct data model that nobody can describe in terms of "what I actually do on a Tuesday" has failed at adoption even if it's never failed a security review. `Warranty_Claim__c`'s lifecycle maps onto exactly four real moments: intake (a rep creates the record from a customer's call or email, populating `Product__c`, `Purchase_Date__c`, `Issue_Description__c`, and `Region__c`), automated routing (`Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing`, a record-triggered Flow, fires on insert and assigns the claim based on `Region__c` without any manual forwarding), human review (a Service Rep works the claim, using the Account/Contact lookups to pull purchase and customer history), and resolution (the rep sets `Resolution_Notes__c` and, if approved, `Claim_Amount__c`, then moves `Status__c` to Closed).

The permission-set split is what makes that lifecycle actually safe to run at scale: `Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep` grants the access a rep needs to work their own region's queue, while `Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager` layers on the visibility `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` now correctly extends up the Role Hierarchy -- a manager sees their whole region's claims, not just their own, which is precisely the capability Lesson 17's fix restored. Neither permission set grants more than its role needs; a rep working the West region queue has no standing reason to see East region claims, and the sharing model enforces that by default rather than by convention.

The honest boundary matters just as much as the workflow itself. No customer-facing self-service portal exists -- a customer cannot check `Status__c` on their own claim; every status update still has to come from a rep on the phone or by email, a real, named V2 idea since the object was first scoped. No automated SLA escalation exists either -- the "aging past SLA" view on the Warranty Claims by Region report surfaces claims sitting open too long, but nothing proactively reassigns or alerts on them; a manager has to actively check that view. Stating both plainly here, in the same conversation as the real workflow that does work, is what keeps today's description of the system accurate rather than aspirational.

```

```

IF the issue is ambiguous or high-value:
    -> flag to the regional manager before closing -- this is a
       judgment call a single rep shouldn't make alone

       move to Closed
```

No customer can log in anywhere to check their own claim's `Status__c`. Neither is a hidden gap -- both are real, scoped-out boundaries.

```

1. A customer-facing self-service portal where a customer logs in
   and sees their own claim's Status__c directly, instead of
   calling or emailing a rep for an update.
2. Automated SLA escalation: a claim open past a defined threshold
   automatically alerts or reassigns, instead of depending on a
   manager actively checking the aging view.
Both are real ideas worth building -- neither exists in this system
today.
```

## Step 6 -- Close the loop on what this means for Hannah's and Tobias's teams

Both managers now get an accurate daily read on their own region because the Role Hierarchy fix made `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` actually work -- the workflow above was always correct; what changed in Lesson 16 was only who could see it.
