lessons.title: Writing the Admin Documentation and Handoff
lessons.summary: The real admin documentation for the warranty-claim system -- object, security model, Flow, and reports as built; the role-hierarchy incident documented as a named lesson learned; ownership by Devon Okafor; and the standing Role-Hierarchy-vs-org-chart review process for any future team change.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A Salesforce org that only Devon Okafor fully understands is a liability the moment Devon is unavailable -- out sick, on vacation, or simply handed a different project. This video writes the document that prevents that: real admin documentation for the warranty-claim build, covering what was built (`Warranty_Claim__c`, its fields, OWD Private, the `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` sharing rule, the `Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing` flow, the two permission sets, and the Warranty Claims by Region report and dashboard), the role-hierarchy incident written up as a named lesson learned rather than buried, who owns it day to day, and the standing review process that now runs any time a new role or team structure gets introduced anywhere in the org.

This is the artifact that turns "Devon knows how this works" into something any future admin, or anyone auditing Cascade Ridge Outfitters' Salesforce security model, can actually read and act on without a meeting -- and specifically, something that stops this exact class of confusion (can a rep own their own records versus can a manager see their team's records) from quietly happening again somewhere else in the org.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a manual taped inside a store's back office that doesn't just say what the new cash register system does, but also explains a mistake that happened when it was first set up -- the manager's name got listed wrong on the org chart -- and exactly how that got fixed, plus who's in charge of the system now and what to check before setting up any new team in the future. A new office manager who's never seen this system before can read that manual and avoid making the exact same mistake.

That's what this documentation is for Cascade Ridge Outfitters. It writes down, in plain language, what was actually built, the one real mistake that happened early on and how it got fixed, who's responsible for keeping it running, and a simple checklist to run through any time a new team or manager gets added -- so the next person who touches this system doesn't have to start from zero or repeat the same mistake Hannah and Tobias ran into.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Admin documentation earns its place in the handoff only if it's written for someone who wasn't in the room for any of the last eighteen videos -- which means every claim in it has to be specific and checkable, not aspirational. "We built a warranty claims object with security" is not documentation; "`Warranty_Claim__c`, OWD Private, extended to regional managers by `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility`, a criteria-based sharing rule keyed on the Role Hierarchy, with reps and managers governed by two distinct permission sets" is.

The limitations section is the part most admin handoffs get wrong by omission, and it's the part that matters most here specifically because of what already happened. Documenting the role-hierarchy incident as a named lesson learned -- Hannah Reyes and Tobias Lindgren placed as Role Hierarchy peers of their own Service Reps instead of parent roles above them, so `Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility` had nothing to extend for either manager -- isn't an embarrassing footnote, it's the single most useful entry in the document for whoever builds the next role or team structure in this org, because it tells them exactly which assumption not to make: that getting record ownership right (a rep owns their own claims) automatically means managers can see their team's records. Those are two separate questions, and this incident is the proof.

Ownership needs the same specificity a model card would demand of a data science team: Devon Okafor owns the warranty-claim system itself -- the object, the sharing rule, the Flow, the permission sets, and the reports -- and is the point of contact for any change to any of them. The standing review process has to be written as an actual, runnable checklist, not a vague intention: before any new role or team structure goes live anywhere in this org, someone checks the real org chart against the Role Hierarchy tree in Setup, specifically verifying manager-to-team visibility, not just confirming that individual records are owned correctly. Stating that this is a manual checklist step tied to future changes -- not an automated or scheduled audit -- is itself an honest limitation worth naming here, not implying a rigor that doesn't exist.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State what was built, specifically

```
ADMIN DOCUMENTATION -- CASCADE RIDGE OUTFITTERS WARRANTY CLAIMS

Object: Warranty_Claim__c
  Fields: Status__c, Product__c, Purchase_Date__c,
          Issue_Description__c, Resolution_Notes__c, Claim_Amount__c,
          Region__c, plus lookups to Account and Contact
  OWD: Private
Sharing: Warranty_Claim_Manager_Visibility -- a sharing rule that
  extends visibility up the Role Hierarchy to regional managers
Automation: Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing -- a Record-Triggered Flow
  that routes a new claim to the correct regional queue based on
  Region__c
Security: Warranty_Claim_Service_Rep / Warranty_Claim_Service_Manager
  permission sets, governing claim-level access by role
Reporting: "Warranty Claims by Region" report and dashboard,
  including an aging/SLA view
```

## Step 2 -- Document the role-hierarchy incident as a named lesson learned

```
KNOWN LIMITATIONS -- LESSONS LEARNED

1. ROLE HIERARCHY MISALIGNMENT (found and fixed shortly after
   go-live): Hannah Reyes (West Region Service Manager) and Tobias
   Lindgren (East Region Service Manager) were originally placed
   directly under "VP of Customer Service" as peers of their own
   Service Reps, not as roles above them. Warranty_Claim_Manager_
   Visibility was built correctly and needed no changes -- but a
   sharing rule that extends visibility up the Role Hierarchy has
   nothing to extend when the hierarchy doesn't reflect who actually
   manages whom. Both managers independently reported their regional
   dashboards showing almost none of their own team's claims; Devon
   diagnosed it by checking the actual Role Hierarchy tree in Setup,
   not the sharing rule.
   FIX: created "Regional Service Manager -- West" and "-- East"
   roles directly under VP of Customer Service; reassigned both
   managers and every Service Rep to report correctly.
   TAKEAWAY: record ownership (who owns a record) and hierarchy-
   based visibility (who can see records owned by people below them)
   are two separate questions. Getting the first right never
   guarantees the second is right too -- check both, every time.
2. No customer-facing self-service portal (named V2 idea since
   initial scoping).
3. No automated SLA escalation on aging claims (manual dashboard
   check today).
```

## Step 3 -- State ownership plainly, by name

```
OWNERSHIP
  System owner (object, security, Flow, reports): Devon Okafor,
    Salesforce Administrator -- point of contact for any change
  Business sponsor: Marisol Fontaine, VP of Customer Service
  Regional owners of day-to-day use: Hannah Reyes (West),
    Tobias Lindgren (East)
  Sales-side stakeholder: Renee Castellano, Sales Operations Lead
```

## Step 4 -- Write the standing Role-Hierarchy review process as a runnable checklist

```
BEFORE ANY NEW ROLE OR TEAM STRUCTURE GOES LIVE:
  1. Pull the real org chart for the team or role being added.
  2. Open Setup > Role Hierarchy and compare the tree against that
     org chart, role by role.
  3. Specifically check manager-to-team visibility -- would a
     manager at this new role actually see records owned by the
     people below them? Don't stop at confirming reps own their own
     records correctly; that was never the part that broke.
  4. If any sharing rule depends on this part of the hierarchy,
     confirm it still extends the way it's supposed to once the new
     roles are in place.
  5. Get the regional or team manager to confirm their own dashboard
     shows what it should, before calling the rollout done.
This is a manual checklist step tied to any future change -- not an
automated or scheduled audit. If a future reorg happens without
anyone remembering to run it, this same class of bug could recur.
```

## Step 5 -- Store it where the next person will actually find it

Save this documentation to the team's shared admin wiki, link it from the `Warranty_Claim_Auto_Routing` flow's own description field, and walk Renee Castellano through it directly -- she's the Sales-side stakeholder most likely to be asked about this system by someone outside Service.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Shipped, What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the Cascade Ridge Outfitters warranty-claims build -- what's genuinely live and in use, and the three real gaps left for a future phase. Series complete.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and like the engagement it closes out, it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Cascade Ridge Outfitters went from warranty claims tracked by email and memory, with no systematic visibility for anyone, to a validated, secured, auto-routing `Warranty_Claim__c` system -- built, hit a real role-hierarchy visibility bug a few weeks after go-live, fixed without touching the sharing rule that was already correct, and now genuinely in daily use by roughly 150 people across Sales and Service.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what's still manual, still a human's responsibility, or still not built, so whoever maintains this org next isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud. Three real gaps get named plainly: no customer-facing self-service portal, no automated SLA escalation, and no automated periodic audit of the Role Hierarchy against the real org chart. None of them are failures. All three are honest, scoped-out boundaries of what this V1 build was ever meant to cover.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months helping a store set up a much better system for tracking broken-product claims -- claims that used to live on sticky notes and in people's email now flow automatically to the right team and get tracked all the way through. It's genuinely better than before. But a good consultant doesn't just hand over the keys and call it perfect -- they say plainly that customers still have to call in rather than checking a claim online themselves, nothing yet automatically flags a claim that's been sitting too long, and nobody has set up a recurring check to make sure the org chart in the system still matches the real one if the company reorganizes again.

That's this whole video, for Cascade Ridge Outfitters. The system itself is real, it works, and it's genuinely helping the Service team today. But a customer still has to call or email to check on their claim, an overdue claim still depends on a manager noticing it, and the kind of mix-up that happened with Hannah's and Tobias's dashboards could still happen again somewhere else in the org if nobody remembers to run the review checklist the next time things change.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most wrap-ups skip: it states the real deliverable plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what's running, and it names the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the role-hierarchy incident -- not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations with a reason. For Cascade Ridge Outfitters, three are worth stating without softening.

First, there is no customer-facing self-service portal: a customer cannot check their own claim's `Status__c`; every update still requires a rep on the phone or by email. This was named as a deferred V2 idea back when the object was first scoped, and restating it here keeps the finished system honestly described rather than overstated. Second, there is no automated SLA escalation: the "aging past SLA" view on the Warranty Claims by Region dashboard surfaces claims that have sat open too long, but nothing proactively alerts or reassigns them -- a manager has to actively check that view, the same manual pattern that let the role-hierarchy gap sit unnoticed for a few weeks before Hannah and Tobias happened to compare notes. Third, and most directly tied to what this series actually lived through, there is no automated periodic audit of the Role Hierarchy against the real org chart. The standing review process from the fix is a real safeguard, but it's a manual checklist step tied to future changes -- it only runs when someone remembers to trigger it. If a future reorg happens without that review being run, the same class of bug -- a correctly-built sharing rule with nothing to extend because the hierarchy underneath it doesn't match reality -- could recur in a different team, with nobody watching for it until a manager notices their numbers look wrong again.

Naming these three is not an admission of failure; overselling completeness after this team already lived through one visibility incident would itself be the kind of trust problem that incident already taught this room to take seriously. The honest version of done is: this solved the specific, real problem it was scoped to solve, these are its real edges, and here's what comes next.
